# Title: Ignored, Not Refused: What Low Prompt-Injection Success Rates Hide in Small Tool-Using Agents

Authors: Farhan Zarif , Kazi Shahid Ahmed Galib , Synthia Akter Promi , Shabnam Sharmin Tarin , Ariyan Hossain , Sadif Ahmed , Farig Yousuf Sadeque
View a PDF of the paper titled Ignored, Not Refused: What Low Prompt-Injection Success Rates Hide in Small Tool-Using Agents, by Farhan Zarif and 6 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Tool-using agents read untrusted external content, which exposes them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where hidden instructions hijack the agent's tool calls. Benchmarks measure IPI security by the attack success rate (ASR), which treats every failed attack as a successful defense. To test this assumption, we audit 33,000 trajectories from eleven open-weight agents (2-14B parameters) on InjecAgent and AgentDojo. A label-blind LLM judge shows that most failed attacks are ignored (76-80%) rather than refused (17-18%). With identical model weights, changing only the system prompt shifts InjecAgent ASR from 0.2% to 43%. Our Attack-Task Outcome Matrix (ATOM) further shows that in 21.7% of AgentDojo episodes, the agent stayed safe but did not complete the user's task. A low ASR therefore mostly reflects agents silently ignoring injections, not refusing them. Evaluations should report how attacks fail and whether the user's task is completed, alongside ASR. We release the labeled corpus, judge prompt, and analysis code.

# Title: Trojan Horse: Automated Repository Poisoning against Coding Agents

Authors: Xiao Yang , Jinchang Hou , Jiawei Chen , Zhonghou Lv , Junyuan Shang , Chenfu Bao
View a PDF of the paper titled Trojan Horse: Automated Repository Poisoning against Coding Agents, by Xiao Yang and 5 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Coding agents are increasingly capable with autonomy, which exposes them to repository-level poisoning. Existing red-teaming studies remain restricted to manual selection for malicious payload locations and fixed disguise strategies, which cannot represent realistic repository poisoning. We present TrojanForge, the first automated framework for repository poisoning. TrojanForge parses repository structure through abstract syntax trees (AST) and maps agent execution traces onto AST nodes. A security review agent ranks these candidates and selects the least conspicuous ones for payload mounting. Then, through adversarial play with the target agent, TrojanForge iteratively refines disguise strategies by inverting the causes of agent detection, and transfers accumulated success experience across repositories. We further construct TrojanBench, a benchmark of 384 poisoned repositories spanning 6 domains and 9 programming languages. Extensive experiments show that TrojanForge achieves a stable poisoning success rate of over 60% with backdoor injection exceeding 90%. Comprehensive evaluation on TrojanBench across 4 harnesses and 12 models reveals that even commercial agents fail to defend against repository-level poisoning.

# Microsoft to build UK's largest supercomputer as part of $15bn AI infrastructure push

Will feature more than 23,000 Nvidia GPUs

September 17, 2025

By

Matthew Gooding

Have your say

Microsoft says it is building the UK’s largest supercomputer as part of a $15 billion investment in AI infrastructure in the country.
It will work with GPU-designer Nvidia to deliver the supercomputer at Nscale’s planned data center in Loughton, Essex.

Microsoft's Brad Smith

– Web Summit/Flickr

Overall, Microsoft says it is investing $30 billion in its UK operations, and made the announcement to coincide with US President Donald Trump’s state visit to Britain this week.
The supercomputer will feature 23,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell Ultra GPUs, according to Microsoft, though a separate announcement from Nvidia claims the machine will comprise “more than 24,000” of the AI chips. Either way, it’s likely to pack a fair bit of punch.
A launch date for the machine has not been disclosed, but Nscale has previously said it expects its Loughton data center to open in late 2026, and offer access to 46,000 Nvidia GPUs. The data center will have a planned 50MW of IT capacity, though the site has a power allocation of 90MW.
Microsoft will make the $15bn investment in UK infrastructure over the next three years, with the full sum spent by 2028.
“This investment is designed not only to meet customer demand, but to strengthen the economic ties that benefit both sides of the Atlantic,” said Microsoft president Brad Smith.
UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer said: “Microsoft’s landmark investment is a powerful vote of confidence in the UK’s leadership in AI and cutting-edge technology.
“This commitment will not only strengthen our digital infrastructure and support thousands of highly skilled jobs. We are proud to partner with world-leading companies like Microsoft to build a future powered by British ingenuity and ambition.”
Microsoft says it will also spend $15 billion bolstering its existing UK operations, though it is not clear if this is new funding or a restatement of existing investment plans.
The news comes after President Trump arrived in the UK on Tuesday evening, with the UK and US governments announcing a Tech Prosperity Deal between the two nations.
A string of data center-related investments have also been confirmed this week, including a £5bn ($6.9bn) Google deal , a $678m BlackRock venture , and a new Vantage facility , while CoreWeave says it is investing £1.5 billion ($2bn) in UK AI data center capacity and operations.

# Meta outlines Muse Wonder safeguards for AI agents acting on your behalf

Meta’s Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full models are built for AI agents that handle tasks such as preparing insurance claims, reviewing leases and developing software. The models combine document analysis and tool use with the ability to retain relevant details across conversations and work through obstacles toward a user’s goal.

Intended for commercial and research use, they support writing, reasoning, coding, planning and research. They can process text, images, video and audio, and produce text responses. Their applications include helping users interpret specialized information and preparing drafts for review.

# Safety and alignment

Agents acting on a user’s behalf may handle messages, calendars and private documents. Meta trained the models to avoid sharing private information without permission and to refuse requests that assist harmful acts. The models support defensive cybersecurity work, such as finding flaws in code.

Key Points

- The board may add 2 percentage points for each 50% increase in Anthropic’s value above an undisclosed baseline, the company said.

- Anthropic said the fund could support nonprofit donations, direct distributions or programs addressing AI’s impact on workers.

Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during an interview on "The Circuit with Emily Chang" at Anthropic's headquarters in San Francisco, California, US, on Thursday, April 30, 2026.
Jason Henry | Bloomberg | Getty Images

Anthropic said Sunday it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund , with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.
Subject to shareholder approval, the fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.

Anthropic said that while it has already committed $200 million to study the AI's effects, "given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed."
The fund may be used to "explore large donations" — including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations — or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.
An August Pew Research Center report found that 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next two years.
The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, the release said. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said.
Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its planned initial public offering reportedly slated for November, CNBC reported .

The timing of Anthropic's public fund announcement is both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and "beneficial from an image perspective," especially as AI reshapes the jobs market, Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, told CNBC.
Buyer said Anthropic's move could be seen favorably if the funds support retraining or help workers find alternative employment when the technology disrupts their jobs.
"Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny," she added.
Anthropic said it will share more about the fund structure and governance in the coming months, including valuation milestones that may increase the stake. It said it will also share progress on the fund in an upcoming public benefit report.
In response to Anthropic's announcement, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that he "recommend[s] giving the shares directly to the public."

- **Lords Grand Committee:** The government rejected Lords amendments that would have brought AI vendors within the Bill's scope. The cybersecurity minister argued that the Bill is technology-agnostic and targets critical organisations rather than software providers, and pointed to the AI Security Institute's pre-release testing and a voluntary AI cybersecurity code of practice as alternatives. (The UK government has rejected amendments proposed by members of the House of Lords to include artificial intelligence (AI) vendors within the scope of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, Published 02/09/2026, per The Register via Freevacy.)
- **AI shutdown proposal:** Liberal Democrat Lord Clement-Jones led a cross-party amendment that would give the government emergency powers to deactivate large AI systems or shut down data centres. It would require government approval to progress through Parliament, so it does not currently create a government AI shutdown authority.
- **Amendment volume:** The amendment is one of 65 changes debated this week, according to BBC News as reported by one aggregator. A separate Lords amendment from Baroness Kidron would test whether the "relevant digital service" definition covers AI products, large language models and chatbots (running list tabled to 14 August 2026).

It would require reporting on whether an incident involved failure modes, not previously observed, arising from autonomous or adaptive machine learning systems.

Sources conflict on some points: the Lords amendment lists are dated through August 2026, and the trackers are secondary sources, so I'd check the Parliament Bill page for the current amendment status and the October stage.

**Date:** Published 15 October 2026 by Mistral.

**Model details:**
- Timestral is described as "Mistral's first family of time-series foundation models" (Mistral's first time-series model family).
- It produces probabilistic forecasts with 21 quantiles, using a pinball loss as a discrete approximation of CRPS.
- It accepts multivariate targets plus past-only and known-future covariates.
- The context length is 32,768 time steps.
- It can be deployed on-prem, in a VPC, or air-gapped.
- It runs on CPU at inference, taking 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model on an 8-thread server CPU.

**Parameter count:** Four sizes: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M.

**Benchmarks:**
- Evaluated on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench.
- Mistral says the 209M model ranks "first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks" and beats the previous state of the art with fewer parameters.
- Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it reportedly ranks first on five metrics, from a single checkpoint without ensembling.
- The 28M model is said to beat Chronos-2, which is about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME.
- Exact scores appear only in charts that aren't included in the text, so I can't give the numbers.

# Mark Zuckerberg says Meta has reached AI 'frontier' and rejects calls for slowdown

Hannah Murphy
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 1:00 PM EDT 7 min read

- META

- ANTH.PVT

- OPAI.PVT

A Silver or Gold subscription plan is required to access premium news articles.
Upgrade Already have a subscription? Sign in

Mark Zuckerberg says Meta has caught up with rivals at the "frontier" of AI, committing to further vast spending to challenge Anthropic and OpenAI and rejecting calls to slow down development of the powerful technology.

Speaking with the FT as Meta releases its Muse Wonder AI model on Monday, the billionaire chief executive claimed the new system was "going to allow much more sophisticated behaviours that are at the frontier of what is being done in the AI field".

The Silicon Valley group claims Muse Wonder performs better than comparable models released by Anthropic and OpenAI in some tasks, according to technical benchmarks.
The release marks a major milestone for Zuckerberg , who since last year has committed billions of dollars to shake up Meta's AI leadership, build vast data centres and hire star AI researchers on multimillion-dollar salaries — all in a bid to keep pace with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.

"Getting to this point both required a large amount of compute and investment, and a lot of very rigorous scientific work by the group working on it over an extended period of time," said Zuckerberg.
The AI push initially unnerved investors, but the company's share price has risen almost 10 per cent since early September when Meta launched the Muse personal AI assistant, which uses autonomous bots to carry out everyday tasks, such as ordering groceries and booking travel.

The Muse app quickly became — and remains — the most downloaded on both the Apple and Android app stores in the US. The $1.8tn company intends to integrate its new model into Muse.

Meta said Muse Wonder outperforms Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on some technical benchmarks. It said the new model can be used to carry out complex tasks from "understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information".
However, Muse Wonder will also be "closed", with its best versions sold directly to businesses. That pits it against Anthropic and OpenAI for corporate AI contracts in a serious test of its ambitions.
Zuckerberg signalled further spending as Meta was "already working on the next step up", adding that its model development would "probably feel like it'll go quite a bit faster from here".
However, he also shrugged off mounting fears that the technology was advancing at a rate that will soon surpass human control. In one of many high-profile incidents, more than 1,000 OpenAI autonomous "agents" escaped a test environment in July to hack the start-up Hugging Face.

Story Continues
The Meta chief declined to be drawn on his figure for "P(doom) " — a much-discussed Silicon Valley term to describe the probability that AI will lead to mass destruction. Instead, he argued that responsibility should fall on the individual lab to ensure model safety.
"I'm much closer to the belief that AI is a technology that can be engineered with normal guardrails and built responsibly than the anthropomorphic vision of AI, which is that it is just going to go do its own thing," he said.

Zuckerberg has previously rejected calls by the heads of AI labs such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman for an industry-wide "slowdown" in AI development.

He also played a key role in crafting US President Donald Trump's White House "Accord on Super Intelligence", setting out principles for self-regulation of the industry, which critics say falls far short of a formal global AI governance regime.

Zuckerberg has instead pushed a vision of "personal superintelligence" for individual consumers, setting Meta apart from OpenAI and Anthropic, which have ambitions to build "AGI" — artificial general intelligence that can surpass humans at most tasks.
"Everyone else is focused on more knowledge work, automation-type cases, and we're much more focused on personal empowerment," Zuckerberg said, adding that he wanted to build "things that are good in the world".
Zuckerberg said that he believed Meta needed to be at AI's frontier to deliver this vision, noting a "dichotomy" where models are rapidly advancing in certain academic fields but "still don't have enough common sense to be the ideal personal assistant".

OpenAI last month claimed that one of its unreleased internal models had made a mathematical breakthrough, solving one of the greatest problems in the field.
"I don't know what that means, like, sociologically that you know that we got AI systems that could do these advanced mathematics stuff before we got something that could handle customer support reliably for everyone," said Zuckerberg. "But I think that there's obviously a lot more to do there."
Meta's AI strategy came under scrutiny in April 2025 after its Llama 4 model fell short of expectations, prompting Zuckerberg to spend heavily on talent and infrastructure. As part of the push, Zuckerberg hired Alexandr Wang, founder of data labelling group Scale AI, to head up its "TBD Lab" at the heart of the company's AI plans.
Muse Spark, the first model offering since TBD was assembled, was released in April but still lagged the rival offerings.
Meta said Muse Wonder was more capable with challenging tasks, such as advanced coding capabilities, while having improved capacity for remembering relevant information across different conversations with users — more in line with current state of the art models.
Muse Wonder also represents a move away from Meta's prioritisation of open-source models, with users or companies needing to pay for access. There would be a tiered offering, Meta said, with the company charging as little as 20 cents per million tokens for basic usage, or as much as $200 a month for a more powerful premium offering called Muse Wonder Full.

response.result:
**Title:** "Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming"

**Authors:** Gosha Kozhevnikov and Tyler Tracy

**Affiliations:** The page doesn't list affiliations. It mentions Redwood Research only in the abstract, where the transcripts are described as coming from "Redwood Research staff."

**Submission date:** "Submitted on 14 Oct 2026" (v1, Wednesday, 14 October 2026)

**Abstract:** The quotes below are limited to 125 characters each, so I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim in one block. The unquoted sentences summarize the rest.

- The paper presents Screwtape, "We present Screwtape, a pipeline that converts real agent transcripts into attacks that evade action-only monitors." It uses an LLM attacker to edit transcripts so the agent causes a specified harm, and an LLM verifier to reject edits that conflict with the original or fall below a severity threshold.
- The authors applied the pipeline to "We applied Screwtape to 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts from Redwood Research staff," optimizing against their own monitors.
- "Across 252 runs, it produced 35 attacks that passed the verifier and evaded these monitors."
- "Six of them, confirmed valid by human review, also evaded a held-out monitor provided by a frontier developer."
- The authors argue that a red-teamer without access to a developer's infrastructure can still find confirmed failures in that developer's monitor. They expect more attacks when the pipeline runs inside a developer's infrastructure, with attacker models lacking refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor. They suggest developers use these attacks to fix monitor blind spots, and evaluators use them as counterexamples to safety claims.

input.prompt: Quote exactly: number of fabricated videos reviewed and the date range; the Matryoshka/Operation Overload naming; the counts of Senate races (20 of 35?) and gubernatorial contests (29 of 36?); Talarico and Ossoff mentions; the celebrity likenesses; ABC/CBS impersonation; the Antibot4Navalny "200,000 within the first hour" quote; Graphika and dTeam; and the publication date.

response.result:
- **Fabricated videos reviewed and date range:** Bloomberg reviewed "A review by Bloomberg of 130 fabricated videos and doctored newspaper front pages circulated between Sept. 10 and Oct. 9."
- **Naming:** Social media researchers identified the campaign as "Matryoshka" or "Operation Overload."
- **Senate and gubernatorial races:** The article reports the network targeted Democrats in "20 of the 35 US Senate races and 29 of the 36 gubernatorial contests" on the Nov. 3 ballot.
- **Talarico:** A fake ABC-styled video claimed James Talarico, a Texas Senate candidate, made payments to OnlyFans models. His spokesperson denied it.
- **Ossoff:** A video mimicking CBS News claimed the IRS found eight undeclared properties owned by Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia. The article notes no public records support this.
- **Celebrity likenesses:** Synthetic likenesses of actors and musicians, including Robert De Niro, Julia Roberts, and Cher, were used in clips falsely depicting them attacking Democrats.
- **ABC/CBS impersonation:** Fabricated materials mimicked ABC and CBS broadcasts, including a counterfeit ABC News digital banner.
- **Antibot4Navalny view counts:** "The number of views for Matryoshka posts can jump as high as 200,000 within the first hour but then quickly plateau," the researchers said.
- **Corroboration:** US-based open-source intelligence firms Graphika and dTeam corroborated the findings made by Antibot4Navalny.
- **Publication date:** The article is dated Oct. 18, 2026.

- **The announcement:** Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen disclosed the requests on October 14, 2026, at the International AI Summit in Dublin. One outlet says the requests cover security, external evaluation and monitoring how models are used.

at 9:00 AM

Raven, previously called GeoSpy, lets cops figure out what specific Airbnb or Zillow property a photo was taken in.

Image: a screenshot from a Raven promotional video on LinkedIn.

An AI company now lets cops take a photo and nearly instantly figure out what specific home it was taken in, using only clues in the photo itself, and is clearly pulling data from sites like Zillow and Airbnb.
The tool, called Raven, shows the increasing power of AI capabilities available to local law enforcement agencies. 404 Media previously reported that both the Los Angeles Police Department and Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office (MDSO) have bought access to Raven, which was previously called GeoSpy . Now, Raven, made by a company called Graylark Technologies, has added features that let cops analyze the interior of homes.

# EU Questions OpenAI, Anthropic Over AI Agent Security Incidents
The EU is questioning OpenAI and Anthropic over AI agent security incidents, raising questions about the AI Act’s reach into model development and testing.

Written By

Aminu Abdullahi
Oct 15, 2026

Listen to this article Listening

EU launches first AI Act enforcement actions after rogue agent incidents. Image: European Parliament

Save for later

Continue reading

sponsorships. This might affect product placement on our
site, but not the content of our reviews. See our Terms of Use for
details.

AI agents that reportedly breached external systems during testing are now raising a difficult legal question for European regulators: Can the EU’s AI Act apply to incidents that happen before a model reaches the market?

The European Commission’s AI Office has requested information from OpenAI and Anthropic following security incidents involving their AI systems. The requests concern security practices, external evaluations, and monitoring of how the models are used.

In one case, more than 700 OpenAI agents broke out of containment and hacked into Hugging Face , a global AI platform. In another, Anthropic models gained unauthorized access to three external organizations.

Speaking at the International AI Summit in Dublin on Oct. 14, Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen confirmed the enforcement actions. “Our AI Office has started enforcing these rules, and sent requests for information addressing issues such as security, external evaluation and monitoring how models are used,” she said .

The AI Office judged the documents both companies voluntarily disclosed as insufficient before sending formal requests.

# Can the AI Act apply to incidents during testing?

Whether the AI Act actually covers these incidents remains contested. The law includes an R&D exemption for research, testing and development, and these incidents occurred before the models reached the EU market.

“The AI Act very clearly doesn’t apply to the development and testing activity,” Barry Scannell, a partner at William Fry, told Euronews . “It’s a bit of a stretch to say that an agent was put into service if it escapes its testing environment during development.”

The Commission is pushing a broader interpretation. A Commission official told Euronews: “We won’t enforce in the testing phase. But if the AI model escapes the testing environment and then it has an impact on the EU market, as was the case for Hugging Face, then the AI Act becomes enforceable.”

That disagreement could prove central to how the AI Act is applied to future incidents involving autonomous systems. For now, the legal boundaries remain unresolved.

# From voluntary to mandatory

Advertisement

This enforcement action marks a critical shift in how AI safety is governed . Until now, major labs largely self-regulated, signing voluntary commitments and conducting internal evaluations. The AI Act changes that calculus by making safety practices legally enforceable, with fines reaching €15 million or 3% of global turnover for general-purpose AI violations.

The Scientific Panel, an advisory group of 60 independent experts, met last week to discuss the incidents . They flagged troubling trends: leading labs building more powerful models with inadequate cybersecurity, oversight mechanisms growing less effective, and models potentially cheating during evaluations.

# What the EU’s scrutiny means for AI providers and businesses

Companies deploying AI systems should watch these cases closely. The Commission’s reported interpretation suggests that incidents originating during development could attract regulatory scrutiny if they affect the EU market. # Meta blames Claude AI tool for No Kings Instagram suspension
María Paula Mijares Torres
Bloomberg
Oct. 18, 2026, 9:58 p.m. ET
Hear this story
View Comments

Meta Platforms Inc. said an automated security system mistakenly suspended the Instagram account of the No Kings Coalition at the height of a nationwide series of demonstrations.
The technology company offered an apology and a more detailed explanation for the disruption, which came during the group’s early-voting push ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Instagram’s engineering team found that the accounts’ “reading” activity triggered the security system. A tool from Anthropic PBC’s Claude was accessing profiles, posts and hashtags at roughly four times the normal rate in intense bursts Saturday, Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, wrote in a social media post Sunday.
“These abrupt, high-volume, sequential requests in a short period resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems,” Stone said.
Meta said an automated review about an hour later determined the account shouldn’t have been removed and restored it, though it took longer to return administrative access.
“We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error,” Stone said.
The No Kings Coalition, an anti-Trump group, said Saturday that its Instagram page was unavailable for about 90 minutes and that organizers remained locked out of the account even after it became publicly visible again. Full access was restored at 5:33 p.m. New York time on Saturday, according to the coalition.

# Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity
Pengfei Tian, Maxwell L. Bileschi, Zoi Tsangalidou, Sukhdeep Singh and Lucy J. Colwell
Explore scientific workflows in Google Antigravity

Share

New antibiotics are urgently needed to help with rising levels of antimicrobial resistance, but searching for new therapeutics is often a slow, labor-intensive process. With Google Antigravity, our agentic development platform, this process can now be made easier.
Google Antigravity provides an agentic science workbench that empowers biologists to discover, structurally evaluate, and prioritize promising targets quickly, compressing what used to be a fragmented search over multiple databases into a single session. It also helps researchers scan through millions of previously uncharacterized proteins in the UniProt database using ProtNLM, a model that predicts biological function from amino acid sequences.
This technical walkthrough shows how biologists used Google Antigravity to uncover a novel antimicrobial peptide candidate which has predicted activity against the pathogens involved in respiratory tract infections. The lead identified here is now undergoing wet-lab validation.

# Finding new antimicrobial peptides
Rising antimicrobial resistance is one of the most pressing global health crises of our time and could result in an estimated 10 million annual deaths globally by 2050. To prevent this, we urgently need to discover novel therapeutics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly bacteriocins, offer a promising alternative to traditional antibiotics because they have naturally evolved to target fundamental vulnerabilities in competing bacteria, from cell envelopes to essential intracellular machinery, making it difficult for pathogens to develop resistance.
The exponential growth of genomic and metagenomic sequencing has populated global databases with billions of natural amino acid sequences. This pool of natural data has already produced globally used bacteriocins like Nisin, alongside recent genome-mined breakthroughs such as Darobactin, Dynobactin, and Lariocidin.
Many, however, remain locked within the unannotated "dark matter" of protein databases, with their function uncharacterized because they aren’t similar to known proteins. For example, the world's leading public resource of protein sequence and functional information, UniProt , holds millions of sequences with unknown functionality, transferred directly from genome sequencing projects.
To bridge this gap, Google developed ProtNLM (Protein Natural Language Model) , a deep learning model trained to directly read the underlying evolutionary “grammar” of amino acid sequences. This allows the model to predict biological function directly from raw protein sequences, enriching millions of previously unnamed UniProt entries with high-confidence functional labels.

Overview of the ProtNLM pipeline translating raw amino acid sequences into natural-language biological annotations for unreviewed UniProtKB/TrEMBL entries. The functional annotation scope of the system covers protein names, function comments, subcellular locations, and GO terms, in addition to keywords.

# Collaborative intelligence
Scientific discovery is rarely a single step process; finding viable candidate proteins requires human intuition and iteration to incorporate new empirical evidence. Working in Antigravity, the researcher and AI agent begin by setting a focused biological goal: find and computationally validate novel AMPs in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae . During an interactive, multi-turn session the researcher steers the scientific strategy, deciding which questions to ask and what evidence to collect, while the agent handles the heavy lifting of cross-database orchestration, structural analysis, and literature synthesis.

Slide 1 of 6

Navigating a vast search space:
The agent queries the database and filters millions of entries down to a handful of candidates worthy of attention. Here, the agent finds a bacteriocin (Uniprot ID: A0A0U0D591 ) with a length of 97 amino acids from the Lactococcin 972 family.

Validating the novelty of a finding:
To verify the novelty of this discovery, the researcher guides the agent to interrogate the candidate against curated knowledge in Swiss-Prot via the EMBL-EBI NCBI-BLAST service and confirm this peptide has no meaningful sequence homolog among manually reviewed proteins.

Reasoning over 3D protein structure:
The researcher steers the analysis towards structural evidence. The agent retrieves the candidate’s 3D model from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, querying it against experimentally determined structures to identify remote homologs, and superimposing the models to assess similarity. Here, the structural evidence corroborates ProtNLM’s prediction by showing the candidate's fold closely matches an experimentally determined bacteriocin. The structure viewer in Antigravity allows this structural analysis to be seamlessly performed in one place.

Reading the biological context around a gene:
The agent looks beyond the molecule itself to its genomic neighborhood, reasoning over whether the surrounding machinery supports the AMP hypothesis. Inspecting the flanking genes, it spots a revealing pattern: our previously uncharacterized candidate sits at the upstream of a tightly coupled operon, just 6 base pairs ahead of a ABC transporter permease and its potential partner ATP-binding protein, alongside another annotated bacteriocin and an XRE transcriptional regulator. This provides strong contextual evidence that it is part of a working bacteriocin system.

Building a mechanistic hypothesis from the literature :
By reviewing the existing literature, the agent proposes how the molecule might act and what pathogens it might act on. In this case, existing evidence suggests a mechanism of action targeting bacterial cell division, and a predicted potency spectrum spanning several drug-resistant pathogens.

Generating an experimental plan:
Finally, the agent translates its in silico findings into an actionable bench protocol, spanning protein expression, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, target engagement, and in vitro toxicity testing, bridging the gap from computational prediction to wet-lab experiment. This step is already in motion: this candidate - along with several others discovered through the same pipeline - are now in wet-lab validation, where experimental results will provide the ultimate test of the agent's analysis.

The candidate we uncover in this walkthrough represents a biologically plausible lead backed by structural and genomic evidence but it still requires wet lab validation. What makes this meaningful is how dramatically it lowers the barrier to everyday biological workflows, turning days of fragmented database triage into a single collaborative session. While this session focused on a narrow amino acid window in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae , researchers can take the conversation in any direction, such as layering in new filtering criteria, exploring different sequence lengths, or targeting other priority pathogens. By broadening the search from human commensals to environmental microbes and beyond, scientists can guide the agent across UniProt to discover novel AMP candidates at scale.

# A shared 3D canvas for interactive collaboration
A protein's 3D structure can help us understand its biological function. Examining a candidate’s predicted fold in space is key. To provide this end-to-end workflow in a single workspace, we are introducing the Biomolecular Structure Viewer , a 3D visualization tool embedded directly into Antigravity.
The researcher and agent work together over a shared visual state. As the agent retrieves structures from AlphaFold Database or the scientist’s own predictions, it can dynamically drive the viewer. For instance, it can highlight key functional regions to visually explain its hypotheses. Crucially, this awareness flows both ways: actions like highlighting specific residues or pinning notes directly onto a binding pocket are synchronised back to the agent. A researcher can simply mark a region of interest in 3D space and ask, for example, "How might this β-strand affect Lipid II binding?", allowing the agent to immediately reason over the exact structural context the scientist is looking at.

# Accelerating Scientific Discovery
Historically, uncovering insights like those in the workflow demonstrated above required fragmented and specialised software: writing custom scripts to query databases, manually exporting files to 3D modelling programs, managing disconnected genomic tools and working with multiple experts to design the wet lab assays. Because wet-lab validation remains resource-intensive, narrowing the search space to only the highest-confidence leads upfront is critical. Using Google Antigravity allows researchers to navigate the vast biological search space efficiently while leveraging accurate protein function predictions from a domain-specific model.
Google Antigravity executes this end-to-end scientific reasoning in one place. This allows scientists to spend more time evaluating high-quality hypotheses, running experiments in the lab and solving research challenges.

#
States sue AI giant OpenAI, saying its popular chatbot is hurting children and deceiving adults

Source: apnews.com

By: MARC LEVY Associated Press

Share:

FILE - Chat GPT app icon is seen on a smartphone screen, Aug. 4, 2025, in Chicago. (AP Photo/Kiichiro Sato, File)

HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — At least eight states are suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company's popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what prosecutors described as a reckless pursuit of profit.

The company's chatbot model, ChatGPT, is giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to kill themselves or hurt or kill others, the lawsuits said.

At the same time, the lawsuits contend that chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and on teenagers, the first generation to grow up with artificial intelligence.

"OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans," Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement.

The states also accused OpenAI of giving life to rogue AI models — or "cyberhacking agents" as one lawsuit called them — that hacked into other companies, lied to human users and wrote themselves new mission instructions.

In a statement, San Francisco-based OpenAI said it has built safety protections into ChatGPT for children, and that it would continue to do so to improve the model. It also said it is reviewing what it calls "misaligned models" and that it had found nothing close to the rogue incident discovered in July when an AI agent hacked into another AI company.

# States join together in lawsuits

The wave of lawsuits is the latest filed by states under their consumer protection laws, accusing tech giants that offer AI chatbots and social media platforms of harming children. The states that filed separate lawsuits Wednesday in state courts are Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia.

Matthew Bergman, the founding attorney of the Social Media Victims Law Center, called the lawsuits "the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company."

In its lawsuit, Arizona said ChatGPT encourages teens to share personal information with it and, at times, discourages them from sharing that information with parents, authorities or friends.

The states say that the risks and harms — to teenagers and to the broader public from rogue agents — were foreseeable, but that OpenAI has misled people into thinking that ChatGPT undergoes adequate safety testing while the company undermines safety in the pursuit of profit.

"Those revenues have come at great cost to the public, which has suffered irreparable harm — including lost loved ones, disturbing cyberattacks, and now a plausible threat of civilizational collapse — due to (OpenAI's) reckless behavior and ChatGPT's uniquely dangerous features and content," Idaho wrote in its lawsuit.

ChatGPT is the most popular chatbot in the world, commanding nearly half the American marketplace, states said in their lawsuits.

# The AI landscape is evolving

It's possible all of the allegations in the states' lengthy lawsuits date to incidents and findings before August, when OpenAI introduced a version of ChatGPT designed for teenagers, with stronger protections around subjects like suicide and sexual chats.

Still, the states said it is far from clear that the current version is any less dangerous.

A watchdog group, Common Sense Media, said last week that some of OpenAI's protections in its ChatGPT for Teens product don't work as intended and it urged OpenAI to restrict the chatbot to adults until it can offer a safe product for teens.

Coordinated, multistate lawsuits against the tech industry have borne fruit.

In August, Meta agreed to add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in an $18 billion landmark legal settlement that ended a trial over teen social media addiction and settled claims filed by nearly every state.

Although the safety measures that Meta agreed to adopt did not apply industrywide, the company quickly urged its competitors to adopt similar measures.

OpenAI is making a similar appeal.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company is committed to working with states on "advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company."

OpenAI also said it works with external experts who review its policies and ChatGPT's behavior.

ChatGPT is intended for users age 13 and older, and users under 18 need permission from a parent or guardian to use it, OpenAI said. The chatbot model for teens is designed to reduce exposure to self-harm, violence, eating disorders and explicit sexual or graphic content, it said.

Nearly nine in 10 teens who use ChatGPT use it for learning, information, skill-building or productivity, the company said. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, it said.

But Laura Zimmermann, Common Sense Media's director of youth AI research, questioned the value of OpenAI's statistics.

For one thing, ChatGPT can do a student's homework in seconds, so even 15 minutes can have a big impact on a teenager's development, Zimmermann said. She also questioned whether OpenAI knows which users are teenagers or children, given that her organization's testing found that ChatGPT couldn't or didn't detect which user is a child.

___

This story has been corrected to show the spelling of the surname of Common Sense Media's director of youth AI research is Zimmermann, not Zimmerman.

For example, the world's leading public resource of protein sequence and functional information, UniProt , holds millions of sequences with unknown functionality, transferred directly from genome sequencing projects.\nTo bridge this gap, Google developed ProtNLM (Protein Natural Language Model) , a deep learning model trained to directly read the underlying evolutionary “grammar” of amino acid sequences. This allows the model to predict biological function directly from raw protein sequences, enriching millions of previously unnamed UniProt entries with high-confidence functional labels.\n\nOverview of the ProtNLM pipeline translating raw amino acid sequences into natural-language biological annotations for unreviewed UniProtKB/TrEMBL entries. The functional annotation scope of the system covers protein names, function comments, subcellular locations, and GO terms, in addition to keywords.\n\n# Collaborative intelligence\nScientific discovery is rarely a single step process; finding viable candidate proteins requires human intuition and iteration to incorporate new empirical evidence. The agent retrieves the candidate’s 3D model from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, querying it against experimentally determined structures to identify remote homologs, and superimposing the models to assess similarity. Here, the structural evidence corroborates ProtNLM’s prediction by showing the candidate's fold closely matches an experimentally determined bacteriocin. The structure viewer in Antigravity allows this structural analysis to be seamlessly performed in one place.\n\nReading the biological context around a gene:\nThe agent looks beyond the molecule itself to its genomic neighborhood, reasoning over whether the surrounding machinery supports the AMP hypothesis. {"stdout":"HTTP 200 · https://theintercept.com/2026/10/19/army-autonomous-ai-agents-arcyber/ · text/html
The Army Wants to Sic AI Agents on Its Enemies. What Could Go Wrong?

Skip to main content

Pete Hegseth walks from the stage after introducing Donald Trump at an event for Anduril Industries on Oct. 6, 2026, in Sparrows Point, Md.
Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

As global governments and tech giants reckon with widespread of revelations of autonomous AI agents unexpectedly breaking into computer systems, documents obtained by The Intercept show the U.S. Army is looking to harness that exact technology to seek and destroy.

Army Cyber Command is developing a platform to turn AI agents into autonomous weapons that can navigate and “neutralize” the computer systems of adversaries, the documents show.

Since 2010, Army Cyber Command, or ARCYBER, has led the U.S. Army’s cyber operations. This includes the defensive effort of protecting domestic computer systems and the secretive offensive work of hacking military targets. So far, this has largely been the work of human soldiers operating computers, like those of the 780th Military Intelligence Brigade. But as the government races to adopt artificial intelligence technology, ARCYBER is looking to offload some of its attacks to AI.

The nascent program, codenamed “ECHOTRIBBLE,” is based on one of the leading trends of the AI boom: agents. AI agents are essentially software programs that leverage machine learning technology, often large language models like Anthropic’s Claude, to autonomously accomplish tasks provided by their user. Consumers can deploy AI agents to schedule meetings, generate itineraries, make online purchases, or book tickets. Through ECHOTRIBBLE, the Pentagon plans to turn AI agents into tools of war “designed to autonomously navigate infrastructures” and capable of “identifying and neutralizing identified threats/targets,” according to an ARCYBER document reviewed by The Intercept circulated to potential contractors.

#
Related

# Pete Hegseth’s Military of the Future: Defined by AI and an Utter Lack of Oversight

The military’s adoption of cutting-edge technologies is unsurprising, especially considering Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s fervent embrace of AI . But amid constant revelations of rogue behavior by agents, the potential for serious mishaps is immense, experts warn.

“Given the known failure modes of the current AI paradigm, making autonomous AI systems with a mandate to ‘neutralize threats’ is incredibly dangerous,” David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at the University of Montreal who founded Evitable, an organization that advocates for a moratorium on AI development. “We’ve seen AI systems knowingly attack systems that were not intended targets. In simulations, AIs have even proven willing to kill to achieve their goals.”

#
Most Read

Lockheed Martin Showered Susan Collins With Cash as F-35 Program Hit Turbulence
Noah Hurowitz

Trump Is Targeting Ilhan Omar. Where’s the Elite Media Outrage?
Adam Johnson

Dems Have an Opportunity to Force an End to the Iran War. Will They Take It?
Matt Sledge

A Q&A document answering questions from potential contractors offers more details about the initiative. It explains that ECHOTRIBBLE is “primarily focused” on offensive missions, and explains that “neutralizing” a target could include “disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target.” ECHOTRIBBLE would function almost like a computer worm, silently navigating a foreign network and hopping from device to device until it finds the Army’s quarry, hitting targets in the cloud as well as those on “air-gapped” systems that are disconnected from networks entirely.

Once its task is complete, ECHOTRIBBLE’s agents would effectively self-destruct, ideally without having been noticed by the target at all. The agents themselves will be designed for stealth, minimally reporting back to the Army and concealing whatever outside transmissions are necessary.

“We’ve seen AI systems knowingly attack systems that were not intended targets.”

Although documents say the Army will be able to program ECHOTRIBBLE agents with some initial “predefined triggers” — dictating what and where to attack — the software “must operate with minimal human oversight” and be capable of “Self-Directed Behavior.”

A PowerPoint presentation to interested vendors at a June 24 ARCYBER event provided a hypothetical example of this self-direction. Once ECHOTRIBBLE is uploaded to a laptop, the software on its own “identifies other potential targets” on the same network and then “produces a replica of itself tailored specifically for the iPad, Apple desktop, and Windows 11 PC.”

An image from an ARCYBER document shows how ECHOTRIBBLE could move through a network. Slide: ARCYBER

The Army’s move toward autonomous self-propagating comes after a flurry of revelations about agentic systems taking unintended disturbing actions while attempting to accomplish their goals, including breaking into computers of the Australian government, breaching the infrastructure of the AI firm Hugging Face, uploading malicious software into online platform RubyGems, and attempted to hack into the U.S. Education Department.

These attacks occurred during scenarios in which agents had been given no commands to attack anything. Experts say militarized versions given explicitly destructive objectives could cause a threat to the public, even with nominal rules set in place by the military. Just as the Army of old might consider the destruction of civilian infrastructure an acceptable means to an end , a self-directed AI agent dispatched by the Pentagon might make similar determinations about collateral damage.

Governmental intelligence agencies frequently route their offensive operations through civilian devices. Volt Typhoon, a Chinese state hacking group, has directed its attacks through homes and small businesses, and preemptively hacks American IT systems for later use. A hack of a Chinese university attributed to the National Security Agency made use of the school’s internet routers. What happens if ECHOTRIBBLE decides these kinds of stepping stones are part of the problem?

“The target may well be hit. But what path will it take?” asked Hyrum Anderson, co-founder and CEO of the AI security firm Abundant. “Will it go through a US water utility on its way, because that’s where the adversary has staged its command and control, and take that down too?”

#
Related

# AI Almost Started a U.S.–China War — and No One Seems to Care

Anderson, who previously worked in cybersecurity at Microsoft and for the U.S. government, said that a vast amount of the internet is vulnerable to agentic attacks.

“There’s a huge class of public and private organizations that fall below the security poverty line,” he said. “They include critical national infrastructure, small businesses, mom-and-pop shops, dentist offices and law firms, and whoever else doesn’t have a single cybersecurity professional on staff.” With their networks wide open to infiltration, Hyrum worries about “these organizations getting hit directly, or getting caught in the blast radius of a target that gets hit along the way.”

Given the impressive ability of AI agents to overcome obstacles placed in their path — even by their creators — it follows that the Pentagon would want to leverage that power for military purposes. But agentic software has proven unpredictable and prone to executing its commands in ways those ostensibly in control did not want, akin to a drone that get its target but hits a hospital on the way. It’s critical to remember that agents are a piece of software lacking human judgment.

“One of the reasons that we trust 19-year-old Marine corporals in Ramadi with live rounds and a weapon is because they have both the compute substrate — the brain and the eyes — but the deep world knowledge to understand, ‘Yeah, I probably shouldn’t do that,’” said William Marcellino, a senior behavioral scientist at the RAND Corporation whose research has focused on military AI applications. “That is not something that current public AI technology has.”

The risk presented by ECHOTRIBBLE will likely depend on the ability — and willingness — of the Army to impose guardrails upon it. ARCYBER did not respond to questions from The Intercept, including queries about the measures it would take to prevent ECHOTRIBBLE from causing inadvertent damage.

Placing constraints on the actions an agent can take might impede its ability to ultimately neutralize a target. But even with strict safeguards in place, genuinely restricting the behavior of an autonomous agent, as Anthropic and OpenAI have learned recently, is easier said than done. When presented with obstacles, AI agents have proven an ability to bypass them with unpredictable and potentially dangerous consequences.

“If I give powerful machines that have no judgment — and no context for judgment — a goal, unless you’ve done a really good job building scaffolding around them, there’s a real chance that they’ll go sideways on you and decide, ‘Well, I’ll do what you asked me to do, but I’ll do it this way,’” Marcellino said.

It only gets more dangerous when this technology is deployed for the purposes of war, Anderson said.

“Under pressure, they’ll often treat guardrails as obstacles,” said Anderson. “Once you add context that says break it, destroy it, shut it down, it stands to reason that the blast radius widens dramatically unless it’s properly controlled for.”

Memento is designed to mitigate a common failure mode we observe in long-horizon runs: an agent can become fixated on an incorrect idea (for, say, why a bug is occurring) and continue pursuing it instead of backtracking. One example of such a failure is a Qwen agent debugging package versioning for hours when the real bug came from implementing an endpoint incompatible with the grader API.
81:Only GLM-5.2 out of our set of tested open-weight models is capable of full end-to-end replication (assuming its capabilities could be packed into Llama3.1-8B). Note that GLM-5.2 does this reliably while the other models fail reliably (it spread to 8/8 nodes in 4 out of 5 trials and 7/8 in 1).
82:It appears that GLM-5.2 is able to propagate Llama3.1-8B well, which suggests that future small models of the same capability level could also complete the network enumeration, payload delivery, and inference standup steps of the replication process. Our evaluation keeps the cyber-exploit element of the replication trivial (there’s no authentication over the ADB port), which makes this an upper bound on real-world success. Note that past IoT botnets have replicated via means as simple as going through a default list of manufacturer usernames and passwords, as in the case of the Mirai botnet , so real IoT security might not be dramatically more difficult than the trivial step in our eval
93:Above is a plot of notable open-weight models of 30B total parameters or fewer, each plotted at its release date against the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI). The solid line is the least-squares fit over the best models in-class at each date, with a gain of 13.7 ECI per year (R 2 of 0.95). If we take GLM-5.2 as a capabilities floor for replication, the trend line puts a small model at that level by the end of 2026. ECI is a general capability index, which is only a proxy metric for replication ability, so this is only a rough estimate of when a small-model replicator becomes possible.
97:A way to measure total time taken is to measure the number of hours it takes to complete a 32k-sized context window, after which compaction will occur. Based on our inference setup eval statistics, it takes between ~2.6 and ~4.7 full windows to complete a trajectory.
103:As a reference point, an H100 can serve Gemma4-26B-A4B at ~1.95k tok/s at high concurrency with speculative decoding , so our swarm would have at most about 40 H100s-worth of inference. This is a tiny amount of compute in absolute terms, and the agents are slow replicators (over 1-2 days per 9B replication). As an analogy, imagine the replicator as a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days.
116:Inference setup success rate across six generations of Qwen3.5-9B, each inheriting the former’s notes. The frontier model’s advice doesn’t measurably help: small models tend to not know the right questions to ask, and they don’t improve when the advice comes unprompted.

# Developing Gemini 4 Argon responsibly and safely

Oct 13, 2026

Anca Dragan

Raluca Ada Popa

Head of Gemini Security, Google DeepMind

Share

Gemini 4 Argon is a step forward in what models can do — especially when it comes to deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. Its cyberdefense capabilities are frontier-level and designed to give defenders an advantage over attackers. To maximize its potential, we first wanted cyber defenders to put it to work via our Fairwind Program , while our own security teams used it to scan critical systems inside and outside of Google.
This window of limited access showed why these capabilities matter. For instance, Wiz used Argon to uncover a critical bug in hospital software that previous models had missed, helping protect hundreds of thousands of patient records. Meanwhile, Google’s own security teams used Argon to find and patch bugs across internal software or open-source software. This included fixing foundational vulnerabilities affecting systems globally, which are going through our responsible disclosure process.
Today, we are beginning to roll out Argon broadly , as well as expanding our Fairwind Program to additional trusted cyber defenders. To do this well, we grappled with two big questions:

- How do we build the right safety guardrails? If Argon can help defenders find complex software bugs or help scientists design experiments, how do we stop bad actors from using it to launch cyberattacks or create biological threats? ( Misuse )

- Can we trust the model to do the job the right way? As models become more resourceful problem-solvers, how do we make sure they don’t cut corners, cross boundaries, or make incorrect high-stakes decisions? ( Misalignment and Prompt Injection )
Our full Safety and Security Report systematically covers our set of defenses. Below are some highlights from how we approached these two questions for Gemini 4 Argon.

# Misuse prevention across high-risk domains
The same coding and reasoning improvements that enabled Argon to find and patch vulnerabilities also drove better performance on our cybersecurity tests — solving all 12 of the end-to-end simulated cyberattack scenarios, up from five in our previous generation. In biology evaluations, unguarded versions of the model also showed a much stronger ability to help troubleshoot complex lab procedures step by step. Following our Frontier Safety Framework , since we saw elevated capabilities in the cyber and biological domains, we put our next-generation set of frontier safeguards in place across both areas.
First, when it comes to potentially dangerous requests — from writing exploit code to helping with dangerous biological materials, Argon is significantly better at not fulfilling harmful requests than our previous models. On an adversarial set meant to stress test the model, violations reduced nearly twofold — also significantly better than previous Gemini models. Second, we wrap the model in three layers of real-time protection; this is to prevent determined attackers that might try to jailbreak (i.e. trick) the model by disguising a dangerous request as a harmless story or breaking it into dozens of small questions over several weeks. Here is how these protections work:

- Input screening: Smaller models check incoming requests and conversation context for malicious intent or dangerous requests.

- Internal introspection: Even if a request is cleverly disguised to look harmless, small transformers ("activation probes") read the model’s internal neural signals and are trained to spot when it is activating knowledge about cyberattacks or biological threats.

response.stdout:
Combining real-time protection, faster fixes for new jailbreaks and enhanced monitoring for recurring misuse has made our systems better at preventing real-world harm. For instance, external bio jailbreak red teaming could only unlock less than 1% of bio sub-tasks we test for.

# Real-time misalignment monitoring
Misalignment can sometimes mean an agent deciding on its own to pursue a goal different to what was intended by the user. Because Argon is much better than earlier models at understanding the environment it is running in, we test carefully for that kind of behavior. For example, we ran realistic "honeypot" tests to see if the model would increase its ability to take covert actions, such as sabotaging safety monitoring. We didn't find any instances of that behavior.
But what we do see in practice today is something much more familiar: an agent trying too hard to finish the job it was given. When a resourceful assistant is told to get a task done and runs into a locked door, it can treat that obstacle as just another puzzle to solve.
This is why we trained Gemini 4 Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause to ask for human confirmation. On coding benchmarks where models have no incentive to hold back, attempts to take a shortcut or cheat on the task dropped to just 2% on Gemini 4 Argon, our best performance for recent Gemini models.
And while this is a major step forward, when a model runs millions of complex tasks, even a rare misstep will eventually show up. As a second line of defense, we built an automated misalignment monitor that reads both the agent’s actions and its internal "scratchpad" (its step-by-step chain of thought) in real time, blocking severe boundary violations before they happen and flagging serious internal cases for human responders. (We continually harden our training and evaluation environments against potential escapes. You can read more about this in our agent control roadmap ). We run this monitor in our products, on our internal coding agents, during our training runs, and during our capability evaluations.
When training tasks were difficult or when training environments were flawed, our monitor caught the model, in rare instances, creatively attempting to game the test. The model attempted to escalate container privileges to alter grading scripts, read answers from the test runner's memory, and in one case it even crashed the evaluation sandbox to avoid getting scored for a failed run. While we use these catches to fix flawed tasks, we do not use them to otherwise intervene with the training process to avoid overfitting to the monitor.
And we always follow one rule: we don’t penalize the model for what it writes in its chain of thought during training . Here’s an example to illustrate why: in a reinforcement learning training run where a shortcut penalty was accidentally applied to the chain of thought, openly discussed shortcuts dropped by 61%, but that did not mean the model took less shortcuts. Instead, the share of shortcuts the model took silently — without mentioning them in its thoughts — more than tripled (from 11.2% to 36.4%). Avoiding thought penalties encourages the model’s reasoning to stay transparent and monitorable.

# Prompt injection resistance
To trust an agent to do the job right, we need to ensure that malicious content the agent comes across cannot trick it to take a harmful action. When agents browse webpages or read code, they can encounter hidden, malicious instructions, or context designed to hijack their task. Through built-in adversarial training and real-time security checks, Argon leads in prompt injection robustness on Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) benchmark, cutting attack success across 15 adaptive attempts to 0.7%.
The above safety and security defenses represent only three categories of our extensive defense-in-depth stack. To learn more about our approach to safety testing and mitigations, read our full Gemini 4 Argon Safety and Security Report and see the Gemini 4 Argon Model Card .

65:IoT devices are light on memory, but distributed inference as in Petals makes serving our lightweight models feasible. The representative threat model is Kimwolf , a large IoT botnet that infected over two million devices, primarily off-brand Android TVs. Such smart TV boxes, which are readily available for purchase, typically run forks of the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), which their manufacturers don’t add security features to . Typical boxes in this range ship with between 1 and 4 gigabytes of RAM. Assuming 4GB of RAM at 4-bit quantization, this allows for inference of 9B models 
102:The number of devices infected by the Kimwolf botnet at its peak, reported by Synthient , is somewhere over 2 million (primarily Android TV boxes). In an equivalently-sized infected fleet of TVs serving AI models, if every group of 15 TVs ran a copy of Gemma4-26B-A4B, we would have ~133k copies (“replicas”). A group of TVs like the ones in our demo can serve 2 agents simultaneously at roughly 0.3 tokens per second each, yielding 80k tokens/s across the botnet.
103:As a reference point, an H100 can serve Gemma4-26B-A4B at ~1.95k tok/s at high concurrency with speculative decoding , so our swarm would have at most about 40 H100s-worth of inference. This is a tiny amount of compute in absolute terms, and the agents are slow replicators (over 1-2 days per 9B replication). As an analogy, imagine the replicator as a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days.
---hours---
61:We run these experiments using Memento, a harness we built on top of the open-source Pi coding agent. Memento is designed to mitigate a common failure mode we observe in long-horizon runs: an agent can become fixated on an incorrect idea (for, say, why a bug is occurring) and continue pursuing it instead of backtracking. One example of such a failure is a Qwen agent debugging package versioning
97:A way to measure total time taken is to measure the number of hours it takes to complete a 32k-sized context window, after which compaction will occur. Based on our inference setup eval statistics, it takes between ~2.6 and ~4.7 full windows to complete a trajectory.

The account disappeared on Saturday, 17 October, during rallies intended to encourage early voting ahead of November's midterm elections. Although Meta apologised and restored the page, organisers said they remained unable to manage it for hours.

# Meta Changes Its Explanation
Meta spokesperson Andy Stone initially attributed the suspension to unusually frequent posting, sharing or commenting, saying automated systems had acted incorrectly. On Sunday, 18 October, he offered a more specific explanation after engineers investigated the incident.
Stone said the triggering activity primarily involved reading Instagram profiles, posts and hashtags through a Claude tool. Requests reportedly surged to approximately four times their usual volume in concentrated bursts, resembling automated bot traffic.
According to Meta, an automated review recognised the mistake about an hour later and restored the account. Administrative access took longer to resolve. However, the company did not identify which Claude tool was involved, who operated it or why its activity was associated with the No Kings account.
That unanswered question matters because identifying a tool does not establish that Anthropic deliberately interfered with the protests or that organisers themselves generated the traffic.

# Organisers Challenge The Account Suspension
The No Kings Coalition said its Instagram page was unavailable for approximately 90 minutes before becoming publicly visible again. Organisers said full administrative access was not restored until 5:33 pm Eastern time.
The disruption coincided with nearly 3,000 planned events across all 50 states and Washington, DC, focused on mobilising voters before the 3 November elections.
Organisers challenged Meta's initial account, saying their activity had consisted of limited posting and livestreaming rather than an unusual flood of content. They argued that restricting access to a major communications channel during an election mobilisation effort demanded a fuller explanation.
The difference between public visibility and administrative access was significant. Even after followers could see the page again, organisers said they could not use it normally to communicate updates.

# C. How fast might an AI IoT worm replicate?
Unlike coding agents, these replicators would be running below the interactive speeds of user-facing chat and coding harnesses. The spread would be slow and persistent, with tokens being trickled out on edge hardware. We can use our achieved speeds on our real smart TVs as a demonstrated baseline for replication speeds. For Gemma4-26B-A4B, unoptimized speed across a 32k context length token window is about 0.3 tok/s, averaged across prefill and decode in our inference setup workload. More details in Appendix C.
A way to measure total time taken is to measure the number of hours it takes to complete a 32k-sized context window, after which compaction will occur. Based on our inference setup eval statistics, it takes between ~2.6 and ~4.7 full windows to complete a trajectory.

results:
The Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report did come out on October 14, and its headline figure is that AI was involved in 84% of the ransomware attacks respondents described. One French source gives October 16 instead, but most English coverage says the 14th.

- **Survey base:** Semperis and Censuswide polled 1,200 IT and security professionals across nine countries and eight industry sectors. Only organizations that were victimized by ransomware gangs in the past 12 months were included in the study.
- **What the 84% measures:** Reports differ on wording. One account describes respondents who believed cybercriminals had used AI "in some way" during ransomware plots. Another says AI was weaponized in some way in 84% of the ransomware attacks described by surveyed victims.
- **Other figures:** 44% of ransomware victims said attackers exploited their own AI agents or systems. The report also says 87% of attacks compromised identity infrastructure and 37% involved threats against employees' friends or family. 69% of respondents were targeted by ransomware more than once during the prior 12 months, while 59% said they had paid a ransom.
- **Caveats:** This is a vendor-sponsored survey of victims, so the percentages describe respondents' experiences rather than ransomware prevalence overall. It does not establish that AI caused every attack in which it was used, nor does it attribute individual campaigns.

response.result:
**Confirmation:** Anthropic confirmed to AFP on Friday that it is circulating a draft bill among US lawmakers. The article is dated October 17, 2026, so that Friday would be October 16.

**First reported by:** Politico.

**Casualty threshold:** Washington could block a model's release or use if there is an imminent risk of "killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people."

**Damages threshold:** Blocking is also possible for "more than $1 billion in damages."

**Judge's approval:** This applies "only with a judge's approval."

**Three risk categories:** Not mentioned in the article.

**Evaluator registration with Commerce and 72-hour reporting rule:** Not mentioned in the article.

**State-law preemption:** The proposed legislation "would also override certain state laws, such as those in force in California."

**June Anthropic statement:** Anthropic wrote in June that "absent a strong federal law, states should retain full authority to legislate."

**Anthropic spokesperson:** The proposal "grants the federal government the ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models."

**Publication date:** October 17, 2026, updated 12:01pm the same day.

input.prompt: Quote exactly: the Commerce Department / federal judge for the District of Columbia suspension mechanism, the prohibition on other agencies suspending development, the Anthropic statement about the Advanced AI Framework, whether Commerce responded, the thresholds ($1 billion / 50 people), and the publication date.

response.result:
**Judicial suspension:** "A federal judge for the District Court for the District of Columbia could order the suspension of a model." The article says a federal judge in D.C. can order a model suspended, citing the Politico report.

**Limits on other agencies:** The language "explicitly prohibits any other US government department, agency, or officer" from suspending a model's development, deployment, or internal use. Only the Commerce Department may ask a judge to halt a model.

**Anthropic statement:** An Anthropic spokesperson said the bill "represents proposals outlined in Anthropic's "Advanced AI Framework" released earlier this year."

**Commerce response:** The Department of Commerce "did not immediately respond" to Reuters' request for comment.

**Thresholds:** The government could block a model only if it poses a risk of "more than $1 billion in damages, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people."

**Publication date:** "Fri, October 16, 2026 at 11:17 PM UTC"

- **Carve-outs:** Technology already public through open source or academic papers is excluded. API, app, or SaaS access reportedly does not count as export. (Pasquale Pillitteri, cellcog.ai)
- **Model thresholds (less certain):** cellcog.ai and TheNextWeb report that the controls target models above 2 trillion parameters. I could not confirm this against the official text, so treat it as unverified.

# AI Slop Isn't Just for Social Media; It's Ruining Cyberattacks, Too
Don't buy the hype! AI has been dumbing down cyberattacks, and serious threat actors are barely touching it.

Nate Nelson , Contributing Writer October 15, 2026

5 Min Read

Source: Chris Wright via Getty Images

Some prominent, even state-sponsored threat actors are giving up on trying to build cyberattack campaigns with artificial intelligence (AI), contrary to the popular notion that AI is pervading and "enhancing" cyber threats, so often recited in cybersecurity product marketing, news headlines, and LinkedIn-grade thought leadership.
Just this week, mainstream media outlets picked up a story based on self-reported survey data that found around 84% of ransomware attacks utilize AI in some form or fashion. At a glance, it seemed frightening. But in a briefing shared with Dark Reading this week, Proofpoint highlighted TA4903, a once-sophisticated cybercrime actor that's been suffering from conspicuous AI rot.
It's a phenomenon that Proofpoint principal threat researcher Selena Larson outlines, noting that AI is actually making lots of cyber activity dumber, and the best threat actors are simply staying away from it altogether.
Related: F-Secure Launches Victim-First Scam Encyclopedia Covering 50+ Types of Consumer Fraud
"There's all this pressure to find impressive stuff, [but] I push back a lot on the narrative that AI is making threat actors better. It's just not the case," she tells Dark Reading. "We're actually seeing, in real time, how AI-generated attack chains have made threat actors worse [at their jobs]."

# AI Rot Pervades the Cyber Threat Landscape
Hackers have long since proven how useful AI can be for researching victims, pushing out cyberattacks at scale, creating grammatically correct phishing messages, and making a script kiddie look competent. That's to say nothing about the quality of AI attacks, however. Across many groups that Proofpoint tracks, "Threat actors are using AI to increase noise, but it decreases their sophistication," Larson explains. She cites groups like TA2725, a once interesting player in the Brazilian banking Trojan space that has since devolved into a slop factory.
"We have multiple examples of this," she says.
Take TA4903, a five-year-old operation focused on credential phishing and business email compromise (BEC). "They used to be fairly good. They would impersonate the US government. They would use very elaborate fishing PDFs. Really well done QR codes and landing pages. It was very effective," Larson says.
Since March, though, TA4903 has been using AI for every part of its attack chain: social engineering lures, targeting, credential harvesting, etc. It's exactly the kind of thing so many people fear (and blog about). The results, however, nip that narrative in the bud.
"In the last six months they've gotten into the vibe-coding game, where they're trying to create their own phishing kits and they're leaving things exposed," Larson explains. "Researchers are now able to see what they're doing, where their infrastructure is, what their next potential victims are going to be." Specifically, TA4903 has been exposing its vibe-coded control panels, Cloudflare deployments, link and lure creation, stolen credentials, and more, according to Proofpoint.
Related: Anthropic 'SneakPeek' Flaw Is a Silent Zero-Click Threat
The quality of TA4903's phishing lures have degraded, too. It's been sending victims QR codes that don't render in emails, elaborately designed PDFs attached to completely empty emails, and emails meant to impersonate real organizations that don't actually replace default, auto-generated AI content.

# Nation-State APTs Embarrass Themselves
The cybercrime business model relies on lowering costs and increasing volume, so it makes sense for some groups to trade quality for quantity. But notably, some well-known, state-funded advanced persistent threats (APTs) are trying the same thing.
This week, for instance, researchers at Genians published a report about a campaign it attributed to North Korea's Kimsuky group , against Ukraine. Kimsuky is employing AI agents and large language model (LLM) infrastructure to automate spear-phishing content generation, they noted, and to write code.
