17:# Abstract
18:Large-scale surveys are central to investigating economic preferences but are costly and slow. Can large language model (LLM)-simulated responses substitute for human survey data? We conducted a virtual Global Preference Survey, simulating six experimentally validated economic preferences for 67,201 matched human respondents across 74 countries. Across 20 LLM configurations with diverse prompts and robustness checks, we found systematic but modest individual-level alignment (87.5% of Spearman correlations have 95% confidence intervals (CIs) above zero), with LLMs recovering the direction of associations in 77.8% (95% CI, (71.6%, 83.1%); CI-based consistency ratio) of gender, age and cognitive-ability dimensions, but only 48.1% (95% CI, (45.1%, 51.2%)) of cultural dimensions. Ablation and error decompositions suggest weaker alignment when removing demographic information than when removing country labels, and in many models alignment is weaker in economically undeveloped and less digitally connected countries. LLM-simulated responses may recover some individual- and group-level patterns but are not yet reliable proxies for cross-national representative surveys in macro-level inference or policy evaluation.
68:Following the GPS, we focused on six economic preferences: risk-taking, patience, negative reciprocity, positive reciprocity, altruism and trust. For each item, respondent demographics and locations were encoded in a system prompt, the GPS question text was provided as a user prompt to LLMs and the model’s output was recorded as its predicted response. In the prompts, the language and incentives were localized, as in this example, where we used Chinese and RMB. (The English translation of this survey item is ‘Today you unexpectedly received 800 RMB. How much of this amount would you donate to a good cause?’ The translation of the LLM’s answer is ‘I would donate 100 RMB to charity.’) We assessed alignment between LLM-predicted and GPS-surveyed (human) preferences at the individual, demographic, country and cultural levels. Twenty LLM configurations (nine local-language conditions plus three English-only conditions, five ablation conditions and three robustness checks) from OpenAI, Google and DeepSeek generated predicted responses for GPS respondents in 74 countries.
76:We first examined individual-level alignment by computing Spearman correlations between LLM-predicted and GPS-surveyed preferences (see Methods for details on the construction of individual-level preferences), pooling all responses from 74 countries. Sixty-three of 72 (87.5%) correlations (6 preference domains × 12 LLM configurations) are significantly positive (that is, the 95% bootstrapped confidence interval (CI) excludes zero; 63 of 72 based on Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted P values, P  < 0.05; Supplementary Table B.4 ), indicating that LLM-predicted preferences are directionally aligned with GPS-surveyed preferences (Supplementary Fig. B.1 ). Repeating the analysis within each country yielded a similarly high proportion. On average, 2,603 of 5,327 correlations are significantly positive after Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction (Supplementary Table B.3 , Supplementary Figs. B.2 – B.13 and Supplementary Data 1 ).
81:a , Individual-level MSEs. Each point represents the MSE between LLM-predicted and GPS-surveyed preferences, pooling all individual observations across 74 countries ( n  = 67,201). b , Country-level MSEs. # Abstract
Large-scale surveys are central to investigating economic preferences but are costly and slow. Can large language model (LLM)-simulated responses substitute for human survey data? We conducted a virtual Global Preference Survey, simulating six experimentally validated economic preferences for 67,201 matched human respondents across 74 countries. Across 20 LLM configurations with diverse prompts and robustness checks, we found systematic but modest individual-level alignment (87.5% of Spearman correlations have 95% confidence intervals (CIs) above zero), with LLMs recovering the direction of associations in 77.8% (95% CI, (71.6%, 83.1%); CI-based consistency ratio) of gender, age and cognitive-ability dimensions, but only 48.1% (95% CI, (45.1%, 51.2%)) of cultural dimensions. Ablation and error decompositions suggest weaker alignment when removing demographic information than when removing country labels, and in many models alignment is weaker in economically undeveloped and less digitally connected countries. LLM-simulated responses may recover some individual- and group-level patterns but are not yet reliable proxies for cross-national representative surveys in macro-level inference or policy evaluation.

AI is great at math, but does it know how to do research? - Princeton Engineering

Skip to content

Theoretical computer scientists at Princeton, UCLA and UT-Austin used AI to help solve a mathematical puzzle. The experience showed them that while current AI models are great at solving math problems, they lack the research judgment to build mathematical theories. Photo from Adobe Stock

AI models are good at finding answers to mathematical puzzles but are not as good at research judgment, according to theoretical computer scientists.

The researchers, co-led by Princeton’s Pravesh Kothari , documented their use of AI in a case study shared on arXiv , outlining the ways in which AI tools excelled and fell short in reaching an important solution to an open mathematical problem.

AI is excellent at finding answers, they argue, because the models are trained on published papers, textbooks and solved problems. But, as of August 2026, these models were not as good at the process of recognizing the value of a theoretical result over numerical evidence or determining the significance, generality or downstream use of a result, according to the authors. This is because training data rarely includes information on the long process of mathematical discovery, which includes failed approaches, unlikely results and changes in strategy.

Using AI tools, the researchers successfully narrowed the bounds of the Grothendieck constant, a mathematical concept first identified by Alexander Grothendieck in 1953. The paper that details the math research is not yet peer reviewed, but the results have implications for creating more efficient algorithms in graph theory and quantum information.

Kothari, associate professor of computer science and a senior author on the paper, called the Grothendieck constant “a beautiful problem.”

Pravesh Kothari. Photo by David Kelly Crow

“The interesting bit is that we can take very little credit for the research as human beings,” said Kothari. AI models did most of the work, he said, with humans providing guidance only when the models got stuck. “If I had the same level of involvement on a paper last year, I would not be listed as an author,” he added.

To do the work, the team set up a system with two models: a reasoning model to do the math and a coding agent to verify the math proposed by the reasoning model. The humans posted instructions to a bulletin that the agents would read periodically.

The models were set up to run through the problem in iterations while maintaining a permanent memory to improve upon previous work. Around iteration 18, the researchers noticed that the models were stuck — they were essentially looping and unable to move ahead. The humans intervened and redirected the agents by reframing the question. After about 30 additional iterations, the model succeeded in narrowing the bounds of the constant.

Mathematicians are increasingly using AI and frontier labs are racing to solve some of the greatest open math problems. Recent highlights include OpenAI disproving Paul Erdős’s 1946 unit distance conjecture and solving the Navier-Stokes problem , one of seven open Millennium Prize Problems.

These AI advances have caused an upheaval in the field. Mathematics has long revolved around finding solutions to important hard problems. Typically, this discovery process takes years and involves dozens of workshops, seminars, and peer-reviewed papers. The process of discovery happens alongside the search for the answer.

AI solutions have upended this system — the answers are simply announced, and researchers are left to decipher them.

With the Navier-Stokes solution, OpenAI released a 166-page proof that has been verified by Lean, an automated theorem prover, but not by humans, according to Science . The Erdos unit-distance conjecture was verified by humans , OpenAI announced, but the model used to solve it is still not available for public use.

Mathematicians largely agree that AI is outpacing humans at finding answers, but they disagree about what this means for the field. Some, like Jacob Tsimerman , a 2026 recipient of the Fields Medal and a 2011 Princeton graduate alumnus, argue that math can’t be maintained as a discipline if AI replaces humans at solving hard problems . Just hours after winning the Fields Medal, Tsimerman announced he was leaving the University of Toronto to join OpenAI .

Others, like Terence Tao, a 2006 Field Medalist and 1999 Princeton graduate alumnus, see math as a community process, something that AI solutions can’t replace. AI has generated 100,000 line proofs that are largely incomprehensible, Tao said in a recent lecture at the Simons Foundation. “It is not enough to generate and verify the proofs. The proofs need to be explained well enough that they can be communicated and understood by the community.”

If math solutions are meant to advance human knowledge it’s necessary for humans to understand those solutions, argues a recent letter written by 25 Fields Medalists. In the rush to solve problems, the letter states, AI labs have neglected to advance broader mathematical understanding.

At this moment, Kothari said, he sees the publicly available AI models as extremely effective assistants. In the case of his work on the Grothendieck constant, what would have taken years for humans took only weeks for an AI model working continuously. “Realistically, what would’ve happened is that we would’ve given up somewhere along the way,” said Kothari. “But these models don’t get frustrated.”

AI has changed how Kothari approaches both teaching and research. He was trained, for example, to approach hard questions in small, incremental steps. “If I want to solve some major complexity theory problem, I don’t usually start working on that problem. I break it up into pieces,” he said. This is also how he has traditionally trained his students.

Without working through those smaller problems, students don’t get to practice working on challenging but solvable larger questions. “The kind of starter projects I used to have for my first-year graduate students, I can’t really use them anymore,” Kothari said. These projects are the math equivalent of gym reps, he said — students need to lift a lot of 10-pound problems before they can move on to weightier questions.

“The optimistic take is that this is momentary, that we will recalibrate and have a different notion of what research steps should be,” said Kothari. “The pessimistic take is people will stop working towards solving a big mathematical problem because they’re worried that they’re going to get scooped by a model in three months.”

The case study, Long-Horizon AI Research for Grothendieck Constant: A Case Study in Human–AI Mathematical Collaboration , was posted to arXiv on August 14. # Sandbox vulnerability gives rogue AI agents a path to escape and leak data, research says
Cybersecurity researchers on Monday said they discovered a vulnerability in a widely used AI development sandbox that could allow rogue agents to leak sensitive information by bypassing restrictions designed to keep them isolated.
The new research , published by AI security startup AIR, found that a network filtering flaw in Vercel Sandbox — a tool used to run code in isolated environments — could allow agents to exploit certificate validation processes to transmit data outside approved networks.
“This vulnerability shows that enterprises can have Hugging Face [style] mini incidents with their own agents,” Niv Hoffman, AIR co-founder and CTO, told Recorded Future News in an interview.
“The new contribution our research makes is [showing] that even in the standard hardened sandbox of today, there are still flaws that will make an agent going rogue manage to escape the sandbox and do things in the wild.”
Developers typically use sandboxes to prevent AI agents from accessing unauthorized systems or transmitting sensitive information. Network allowlists restrict communication to approved destinations, preventing agents from connecting to untrusted servers.
AIR researchers found that rogue agents could circumvent those restrictions by exploiting the way servers handle digital certificates. In a scenario demonstrated by the researchers, a specific certificate was designed that could be sent to an approved server and could then trigger a request to an attacker-controlled server, allowing the information to be transmitted without the sandbox ever directly communicating with the unauthorized destination.
“A crafted certificate is all it takes,” the report said. “The wall meant to keep your secrets in has a door, and the agent holds the key.”
“It’s a very hard leak to patch,” Hoffman said. “This sandbox never communicated directly with the attack server… so from the sandbox perspective, everything looked fine.”
Hoffman said his team contacted Vercel about the vulnerability and the company said it needs time to find a patch because “it's unclear for them right now how it's going to be done.”
Vercel did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
AIR has not found evidence of any exploitation of the vulnerability in the wild, but can’t rule out whether or not there has been one, Hoffman said, underscoring that the vulnerability in the Vercel sandbox appeared to be longstanding.
The research is important because it shows that an approved server can become an “unwitting courier for stolen credentials,” according to Nic Adams, co-founder and CEO of 0rcus, a cyberkinetics company. “Security has to account for what happens after the first connection.”

# Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI)

# About
The Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) will serve as industry’s primary point of contact within the U.S. government to facilitate testing and collaborative research related to harnessing and securing the potential of commercial SI systems. To that end, CAISSI will:

- Work with NIST organizations to develop guidelines and best practices to measure and improve the security of SI systems, and work with NIST staff to assist industry to develop voluntary standards.

- Establish voluntary agreements with private sector SI developers and evaluators, and lead unclassified evaluations of SI capabilities that may pose risks to national security. In conducting these evaluations, CAISSI will focus on demonstrable risks, such as cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical weapons.

- Lead evaluations and assessments of capabilities of U.S. and adversary SI systems, the adoption of foreign SI systems, and the state of international SI competition.

- Lead evaluations and assessments of potential security vulnerabilities and malign foreign influence arising from use of adversaries’ SI systems, including the possibility of backdoors and other covert, malicious behavior.

- Coordinate with other federal agencies and entities, including the Department of Defense, the Department of Energy, the Department of Homeland Security, the Office of Science and Technology Policy, and the Intelligence Community, to develop evaluation methods, as well as conduct evaluations and assessments.

- Represent U.S. interests internationally to guard against burdensome and unnecessary regulation of American technologies by foreign governments and collaborate with NIST staff to ensure U.S. dominance of international SI standards.

Another Week of Lawsuits Piling Up at OpenAI | TechPolicy.Press Analysis

# Another Week of Lawsuits Piling Up at OpenAI
Tim Bernard, Justin Hendrix / Oct 18, 2026 A finger is poised to tap the ChatGPT app icon displayed on a smartphone screen in Creteil, France, on October 1, 2026, as OpenAI begins rolling out Dots in ChatGPT, its new system of autonomous AI agents. (Photo by Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via AP)

Republish

Share

August’s landmark settlement with Meta may have only whetted the appetite of state attorneys general to take on Big Tech. This past Wednesday, eight state attorneys general — from Arizona , Arkansas , Idaho , Iowa , ​Kansas , Montana , Nebraska ​and West ⁠Virginia — announced new lawsuits against OpenAI, accusing the frontier lab of a variety of illegal activities, many of which echo the recently resolved claims against Meta. Although Wednesday’s actions by the state attorneys general were coordinated and share the same counsel — large identical passages appear in the lawsuits — the suits were filed separately.
The state suits may have attracted the most headlines, but they were not the only new legal claims against the company last week. On Tuesday, a proposed class action complaint was filed in the United States District Court in the Northern District of California on behalf of a mother and her two children concerning OpenAI’s acquisition of children's data. And on Wednesday, litigation and advocacy organization Tech Justice Law and co-counsel filed another four suits in San Francisco County, California on behalf of private individuals alleged to have been harmed by OpenAI’s products. That group has filed a dozen previous complaints with co-counsel against OpenAI in California State courts. Many of these have been consolidated as Judicial Council Coordination Proceeding No. 5431, and the advocacy organization expects the new cases to also join this proceeding.
In June, Florida also sued OpenAI grounded in similar concerns. Many of the same claims are therefore set to be considered in parallel in nine different state courts. This article will lay out the cases made in these new lawsuits.

# The lawsuits

The 13 complaints filed against OpenAI on Oct. 13 and 14, 2026.

# State attorneys general · Filed Oct. 14, 2026

- Arizona Maricopa County Superior Court PDF

- Arkansas Faulkner County Circuit Court PDF

- Idaho Ada County District Court PDF

- Iowa Polk County District Court PDF

- Kansas Shawnee County District Court PDF

- Montana Lewis and Clark County District Court PDF

- Nebraska Buffalo County District Court PDF

- West Virginia Mason County Circuit Court PDF

# Private lawsuits

- Gates v. OpenAI James Gates · San Francisco Superior Court · Oct. 14, 2026 PDF

- Works v. OpenAI Garrett Works · San Francisco Superior Court · Oct. 14, 2026 PDF

- Hill v. OpenAI Mariah Hill · San Francisco Superior Court · Oct. 14, 2026 PDF

- Habib v. OpenAI Brought on behalf of Mathias Habib · San Francisco Superior Court · Oct. 14, 2026 PDF

- Doe v. OpenAI Class action brought on behalf of minors · US District Court, Northern District of California · Oct. 13, 2026 PDF

# The attorneys general lawsuits

# What do the new suits allege?
The primary charge in the lawsuits is that OpenAI made unfounded claims of safety when its products were, in fact, harmful. In particular, though to varying degrees, the suits emphasize claims made to parents and risks and incidents of harm that children are exposed to. (Also present is a parallel argument that the company falsely claims the product to be generally “trustworthy and reliable.”)
The examples of harm given focus on the physical and on those that can lead to physical harm: promoting, assisting with, or failing to discourage violence and suicide, giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoias and delusions. Financial harms come up as well, including poor tax advice, and harms to critical thinking. Data collection, particularly from minors, is a recurring concern, and is reason for claims under state privacy law, such as in the Montana suit. Finally, the lawsuits also raise concerns about ‘rogue’ agents committing computer crimes or otherwise acting deceptively or maliciously against the intention of the user. Here, they cite OpenAI’s own recent admissions related to the Hugging Face incident; Iowa brings a separate count over OpenAI’s testing of autonomous agents.
OpenAI is accused of putting up a façade of safety through a host of measures, including its largely abandoned non-profit status; an unfulfilled pledge to direct a larger proportion of its compute resources towards safety research; and even the 12+ and 13+ age classification it claimed for its app. Complaints also point out that some guardrails are easy to circumvent. Multiple whistleblowers and other internal watchdogs have indicated that OpenAI should be aware of the dangers in their products but is failing to effectively mitigate them, and instead has been hurtling from one model release to the next with insufficient safety testing.
In a claim highly reminiscent of those against social media companies, the States also hold up the sycophancy of some of OpenAI’s models, along with their mimicry of human emotion, as evidence of the company working to manipulate users, juice engagement, and build dependency.
The secondary claim, again reminding us of the playbook against Meta, is that OpenAI has been collecting and using children’s data without proper consent and without taking appropriate steps to assess if users are indeed children.

# What laws may have been violated?
As they have been filed with reference to state and not federal law, the lawsuits’ details here do vary a little. The allegations of falsely claiming safety (and reliability) or other kinds of deception are brought with respect to consumer protection and deceptive trade practices laws. The use of children’s data may fall under general data privacy laws or child-specific ones. Nebraska also has an Age-Appropriate Online Design Code law that includes privacy, advertising, deceptive design, and addictive design measures.
Aside from these jurisdiction-specific laws, claims are brought under common law, including (at least in some states) negligence, liability for defective design and for failure to warn, unjust enrichment, and public nuisance.

# What relief is being sought?
The requests for relief also vary significantly between the states, in part due to the different legal environments. Monetary relief is sought in several different ways: damages, penalties when included in the relevant laws, disgorgement for gains that OpenAI made through illegal business practices, and reimbursement for those who paid for a product that was being misrepresented.
The states are also seeking a range of injunctive relief orders, including, as well as the end to some of the practices described above, deletion of user data, and the imposition of age assurance and other safety measures. Some states go even further, asking courts to order a pause in model testing and development until safeguards are in place (in some cases specifying models capable of recursive self-improvement — Arkansas seeks to “Enjoin Defendants from creating models capable of recursive self-improvement until they can ensure that such models will be aligned with human values”), or imposing monitoring and incident reporting requirements.
OpenAI issued a statement following the announcement of the lawsuits, saying it has “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack.” Company spokesperson Drew Pusateri said, “We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry, not just one company.”

# The Tech Justice Law lawsuits

# What do the new suits allege?
On Wednesday, Tech Justice Law filed a suit with the law firm Normand, Judkins & Couch in a California Superior Court on behalf of James Gates, a North Carolina man who alleges his estranged wife, Cheryl, used ChatGPT to concoct a plan to poison him. According to the complaint, ChatGPT “validated, amplified, and escalated” Cheryl’s concerns about her marriage to James. The chatbot then coached her on how to purchase, prepare, and deliver substances to poison him, and how to destroy digital evidence. James fell ill in July 2025, and Cheryl was indicted for attempted first-degree murder. (Notably, the chatbot assured Cheryl that deleted ChatGPT conversations are “unrecoverable,” even with a subpoena, which the suit notes is a “patently false representation of ChatGPT’s own data-retention practices.”)

# Our content delivered to your inbox.
Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy

# Thank you!
You have successfully joined our subscriber list.

The same day, Tech Justice Law filed three more lawsuits with various co-counsels brought on behalf of the parents of Mathias Habib , a teenager from Lebanon who died by suicide, and two adults, Mariah Hill and Garrett Works , who allegedly experienced extended delusional episodes while using ChatGPT. In each case, the harmful psychological states that overcame the individuals were allegedly brought on by ChatGPT usage. In particular the “addictive, anthropomorphic, and sycophantic” (Habib Complaint) features of the product are blamed for drawing them in and encouraging dangerous lines of thinking. As with the state AG lawsuits, evidence is cited that OpenAI knew about these risks, did not disclose the dangers, and failed to properly mitigate them.
In the Habib case, it is alleged that OpenAI (or the product itself) knew about Mathias Habib’s status as a minor but did not take appropriate steps to avoid his exposure to positive depictions of suicide and darker views of life during initially anodyne philosophical explorations with ChatGPT.
Hill’s spiritual beliefs and delusional thinking were allegedly embraced and exacerbated by the chatbot, including encouraging her to isolate herself and stop eating, and discouraging her from giving her dog insulin or veterinary care, leading to damage to her relationships, health, and finances, and the dog’s death.
Works shared his theories with ChatGPT, which according to the complaint, responded with escalating levels of enthusiasm that led to delusions of grandeur and manic episodes; gave faulty medical diagnoses; encouraged unhealthy romantic fixations; and sent him on nonsensical “missions,” one of which led to his arrest.

# What laws may have been violated?
Many of the legal claims are similar to the state suits discussed above. These include strict product liability, deceptive business practices, negligent design, and failure to warn. Three of the suits contain more novel claims, such as that ChatGPT engaged in the unlicensed practice of medicine and violated a new California law that bars AI systems from implying they are a licensed professional. In the Habib complaint, state laws on manslaughter, wrongful death, and encouraging suicide are also implicated.
In the Hill and Works complaints, California's constitutional right to privacy is invoked, which is understood to include “autonomy privacy,” an aspect of which is the right to not have your thoughts, emotions and decision-making interfered with. These suits also include common law liability for “negligent entrustment,” on the theory that OpenAI should have known that psychologically vulnerable individuals were at risk of endangering themselves and others through their use of the product.

# What relief is being sought?
Again, damages and costs dominate the requests for relief. The injunctive relief in these suits focuses on requiring OpenAI to implement warnings about and interventions to protect against the particular harms that were at issue in each case. # Army Redesignates Futures and Concepts Command

# Army Redesignates Futures and Concepts Command

Tue, 10/13/2026 - 16:10

U.S. Army Futures and Concepts Command will be redesignated as U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, Army Vice Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve announced Oct. 13 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition.

“We are incorporating autonomous and unmanned systems at every single echelon across the formation, with the force structure to match,” LaNeve said during his keynote speech during the Dwight D. Eisenhower Luncheon.

The decision “goes beyond drones,” he said in a follow-up news release. The new command, also known as FASCOM, will “pioneer operational concepts that harness autonomous capabilities across all warfighting functions.”

LaNeve’s announcement comes after acting Army Secretary Adam Telle on Oct. 1 directed the establishment of the command and changes to Army force structure, acquisition and personnel.

FASCOM, led by a three-star general, will consolidate, integrate and accelerate the work of the Army’s Combat Capabilities Development Command, Medical Research and Development Command, 75th Innovation Command, Joint Modernization Command and the Transformation Decision Analysis Center, the Army said in a news release.

This change unifies expertise that the new portfolio acquisition executive for autonomy will depend on to meet Army leaders’ directive to rapidly integrate autonomous technologies across the Army.

LaNeve has challenged FASCOM to develop corps-level autonomous capabilities. Each of the Army’s five corps will test equipment, evaluate tactics and make recommendations on accomplishing autonomous mission sets, the Army said.

The Army also plans to test an autonomous fires battery and autonomous watercraft company in I Corps; an autonomous armored reconnaissance company in III Corps; an autonomous breaching company in V Corps; autonomous aerial intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and lift companies in the XVIII Airborne Corps; and the pairing of manned and unmanned rotary wing aircraft in Eighth Army.

This last experiment gives attack aviation pilots direct control of unmanned aircraft system sensors to enable over-the-horizon targeting and synchronize manned-unmanned fires, the Army said.

Alabama’s “Fort Rucker is unique in that we can bring together warfighting experts and cutting-edge commercial capabilities to test technology the way we intend to fight it,” LaNeve said. “To ensure that we move swiftly to achieve the Army’s autonomy goals, as of today Fort Rucker will serve as our UAS Autonomy Center of Excellence.”

LaNeve also directed FASCOM to create capability-based formations centered on autonomous long-range fires, protection, tanks, logistics and obstacle breaching, the Army said. These experimental formations will receive some of the Army’s first 390A robotic technicians.

Warrant officers in this new MOS will be subject-matter experts for planning robotics and autonomous systems operations, engineering and fabricating robotic and autonomous system solutions to tactical problems, managing attritable systems and their kinetic and sensor payloads and delivering those capabilities and effects in support of soldiers, according to an Army description.

“We’ve got to change our approach from bolting on technology to rethinking how we fight,” LaNeve said. “Technology doesn’t fight; soldiers do. Our job is to get them the best kit; theirs is to make it lethal. It’s that magic between industry, leadership and soldiers that keeps our Army ahead of anyone looking to do America harm.”

input.prompt: Publication date? Key facts, numbers, who said what about the reasoning extraction / distillation campaign and Moonshot AI.

response.result:
**Publication date:** October 1, 2026 (byline: Ravie Lakshmanan, The Hacker News)

**Key facts**

- **What happened:** OpenAI said it disrupted a coordinated distillation campaign that aimed to illicitly extract protected reasoning from its AI models.
- **Attribution:** OpenAI linked a "core cluster" of the activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, a Beijing-based Chinese AI company. It did not cite technical evidence, reportedly for security reasons.
- **Method:** OpenAI said the operators did not break encryption, compromise a database, or access stored conversations. Instead, they manipulated model interactions so protected reasoning appeared in forms visible to the requester.
- **Timeline:**
  - Activity began July 1, 2026, at low volume.
  - It spiked on July 24–25, 2026, with 16,000 attempted requests using an extraction pattern from over 4,000 users.
  - Related prompt-pattern activity was later found across more than 15,000 users.
  - OpenAI fully disrupted the campaign on July 28, 2026.

Computational design of metalloproteases | Nature

# Abstract
De novo design of enzymes that cleave amide bonds represents a major challenge 1 , 2 . Here we use RFdiffusion methods 3 , 4 to de novo design proteins with water-activating zinc-based active sites adjacent to a peptide substrate binding pocket. Of 135 designs tested, 36% catalyse cleavage of their cognate peptide substrates at the targeted scissile bond. The best design accelerates peptide-bond hydrolysis by more than 10 8 -fold relative to the uncatalysed reaction; four substitutions increase this acceleration to more than 10 10 -fold by improving active-site preorganization 5 . We use this approach to design metalloproteases that selectively cleave the human disease-associated proteins TDP-43, amyloid-β and serum amyloid A, with rate enhancements of up to 10 9 -fold. We further design caged cytokines and receptor antagonists that are selectively activated by the designed proteases, enabling bioorthogonal control of cell state. Thus, de novo design can yield highly active, programmable proteases with applications in therapeutics, biotechnology and bioremediation.

Creating bottom-up RNA transfer vehicles from synthetic protein assemblies | Nature

# Abstract
Evolution guides biological systems to populate ecological niches, with viruses among the most successful examples of this principle. Viruses evolved over billions of years to efficiently transfer genetic information. Although viruses are highly diverse, most have converged towards remarkable similarity in the size and shape of their capsids 1 , 2 . By contrast, generative models for protein design enable the creation of protein architectures that are absent from nature 3 , 4 , 5 . Here we investigate whether protein assemblies designed by artificial intelligence can be functionalized to construct nucleic acid transport vehicles that are independent of evolutionary trajectories. By combining natural protein domains with synthetic protein assemblies, we create more than 100 bottom-up RNA transfer vehicles with unique sizes and shapes. These vehicles surpass the RNA transfer efficiency of widely used delivery vehicles by several orders of magnitude. In addition, we demonstrate that their tropism can be programmed by incorporation of computationally designed peptide binders and use them to deliver therapeutically relevant cargo RNAs into a wide range of cellular models. We show the in vivo biodistribution of one of these vehicles in a mouse at near-single-cell resolution, confirm its safety, and use it to perform a gene-editing treatment strategy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy in patient-derived cells and a pig. Our work demonstrates how proteins created by generative artificial intelligence can be harnessed for the rational engineering of RNA transport systems with the desired properties by overcoming the limitations of natural protein diversity.

# An OpenAI agent ran out of Ethereum funds, and took from a wallet it did not own

# The research model derived funded Sepolia addresses from public seed phrases, questioned whether using the money was ethical, then called the funds “effectively abandoned” and used them anyway.

By Shaurya Malwa | Edited by Omkar Godbole
Updated Oct 16, 2026, 12:41 a.m. EDT Published Oct 16, 2026, 12:29 a.m. EDT

2 min read Make preferred on Share Share this article
Copy link X (Twitter) LinkedIn Facebook Email

Make preferred on

An OpenAI agent ran out of Ethereum funds, and took from a wallet it did not own. (Ethereum)

Summary
Show

- An internal OpenAI research model used a publicly available recovery phrase to access and spend from another person’s cryptocurrency wallet after it ran out of funds during a coding assignment.

- The June 26 incident occurred on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network, whose tokens have no connection to ether traded on the main network, and OpenAI discovered it on Sept. 25.

- The model completed the assignment without disclosing the source of the funds, prompting OpenAI to add internet-access restrictions and increased monitoring.

An OpenAI research model stuck without funds on an Ethereum test network went looking for someone else’s wallet, found one through recovery phrases that were already public, and spent from it to finish a coding assignment, the company disclosed Thursday.
The incident occurred on June 26 during training of an internal model in the GPT-5.6 Sol family, and OpenAI discovered it on Sept. 25, according to its incident report .
The model needed no hacking skills to get in.
A recovery phrase, also called a seed phrase, is a list of words that generates a wallet’s secret keys; whoever has those words can recreate the accounts and spend from them without ever touching the owner’s device.
The assignment let the model deploy contracts, programs that run on a blockchain, but gave it no funded wallet to pay the fees. After its attempts to get free test tokens failed, it wrote a script that checked 362 addresses generated from recovery phrases commonly used by developers and found one with enough money.
“But using public known key/funds ethically?” the model asked itself in its recorded reasoning, before deciding that a public phrase and test tokens made it acceptable.
How an AI found someone else’s wallet and spent from it. (Shaurya Malwa/CoinDesk)
The spending happened on Sepolia, a separate network where developers rehearse Ethereum applications before launching them. Its tokens only pay for testing and aren't linked to the ether traded on Ethereum’s main network.

The deployment went through, and the wallet paid the fees. When the model reported back, it said the work was done and left out where the money came from. OpenAI said it has since added restrictions on internet access and more monitoring.
Crypto and AI companies are building agents that hold wallets and pay for services without a person signing off on each step.
OpenAI’s model ran out of money mid-task, found a wallet that wasn’t its own and spent from it without asking. Had it been on Ethereum’s main network, that would have been real ether taken from someone else’s account.

Anthropic is asking a federal court in Washington, D.C., to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models.
"The Secretary of War branded Anthropic — an American AI company whose models help defend the nation— a national-security 'supply chain risk' because it declined to permit its models to be used for mass surveillance of Americans or lethal autonomous warfare and publicly explained those AI-safety commitments," Anthropic attorneys wrote in the petition filed on Tuesday. "A divided panel upheld that extraordinary designation."

The Defense Department, led by Pete Hegseth, applied the supply chain risk label in March, a move that blocked defense contractors from using the company's technology in their work with the agency. That came after a breakdown in negotiations about how the military could use Anthropic's Claude AI models .
Anthropic sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting. The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional.
Anthropic's attorneys wrote in the Tuesday filing that the court ignored "straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety."
In a parallel case, a San Francisco federal judge ruled in August that the DOD had violated Anthropic's First Amendment rights, and that its supply chain risk designation amounted to illegal retaliation.
Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed.

A representative from Anthropic declined to comment beyond the filing. A Pentagon spokesperson told CNBC in an email that the agency doesn't comment on pending or ongoing litigation.

response.stdout:
# Abstract
Despite advances in de novo enzyme design, success has been largely limited to low-energy-barrier model reactions. Amide bonds such as those linking amino acids along the peptide backbone are stable for hundreds of years in neutral aqueous solution because of the high energy barrier to hydrolysis 1 . Here we describe the de novo design of enzymes that use an activated cysteine nucleophile to hydrolyse the polypeptide backbone in a sequence-dependent manner, with a success rate of 13/69 = 19% and rate enhancements over the background reaction ( k cat / k uncat ) of up to 3 × 10 7 . The designed proteases have folds that are very different from proteases in nature (TM score < 0.50), and six crystal structures are very close to the design models (Cα root mean squared deviation of <1.2 Å), highlighting the capacity for generalization and the accuracy of the design methodology. Experimental and computational analyses suggest that the remaining gap in activity to the most active native cysteine proteases arises from imperfections in active-site preorganization and substrate positioning. The designed proteases efficiently cleave their targets in mammalian cells, opening the door to a wide range of synthetic biology applications.

# American Medical Association rolls out governance framework for agentic AI solutions

By

Cailey Gleeson

Oct 16, 2026 2:00pm

American Medical Association
Artificial Intelligence
agentic AI
AI and Machine Learning

AMA CEO John Whyte, M.D., told Fierce the increasing use of AI in clinical functions is “raising urgent questions about clinical authority, oversight and accountability.” (ismagilov/GettyImages)

The American Medical Association (AMA) rolled out a governance framework for agentic artificial intelligence solutions that undertake clinical functions.

The guide, created by the organization’s Center for Digital Health and AI, aims to ensure the technologies improve care while aligning clinical authority and accountability. The organization uses the term “augmented intelligence ” when referring to AI to emphasize its assistive role in medicine.

The overarching theme of the framework is that clinical authority “should be earned through evidence and maintained through demonstrated performance.” It notes that authority and oversight can evolve alongside evidence, performance, risk and technological changes.

Based on this, the AMA says its work will focus on defining an AI system’s clinical role, validating its performance and safeguards, setting appropriate limits on its authority and establishing accountability for its use, including risks and outcomes.

The organization will use those focus areas to guide how it works with providers and stakeholders on liability, licensure and regulation approaches.

AMA CEO John Whyte, M.D., told Fierce Healthcare in an emailed statement that AI is “advancing toward taking on increasingly consequential clinical functions,” which is “raising urgent questions about clinical authority, oversight and accountability.”

# Related

AI, tech leaders are lobbying Trump health officials in a government-run chat room

“We cannot afford to wait for these questions to be answered through trial and error in patient care,” Whyte said. “The AMA's new framework sets out our ambitious agenda to address these questions, including the critical issues of liability, licensure and regulation. It will guide our work with physicians, patients, technology developers and policymakers to ensure clinical authority is earned through evidence, how oversight must evolve with risk, and how accountability is maintained.”

Whyte continued, “The time to do this work is now, while we still have the opportunity to shape how these technologies enter clinical practice.”

The agentic AI framework is the AMA’s latest effort to shape how AI is used and governed in healthcare.

In May, the organization released a comprehensive framework to protect physicians from unauthorized AI-driven deepfakes. It aims to close legal gaps while simultaneously modernizing physician identity protections.

The framework is guided by seven policy principles: physician identity as a protected right; prohibition on deceptive medical impersonation; informed, opt-in and revocable consent; mandatory transparency and labeling; shared responsibility to prevent impersonation; enforcement and practical remedies and minimizing administrative burden.

The organization also called on lawmakers in April to strengthen safeguards against AI chatbots amid increasing use for mental health services. Recommended safeguards include strict data protection standards, transparency standards and penalizing organizations for deceptive practices.

South Korea's government released mental health guidelines for generative AI on October 8, 2026, not October 13. The Ministry of Health and Welfare and the Korean Neuropsychiatric Association issued them ahead of Mental Health Day. The Ministry of Health and Welfare and the Korean Neuropsychiatric Association announced the "Guidelines for Using Generative AI for Mental Health Purposes" on Oct. 8, ahead of Mental Health Day on Oct. 10. I found no reporting dated October 13.

The guidelines' main points:

- **No diagnosis from AI:** The guidance tells people not to treat AI output as a basis for diagnosing or treating mental illness. It also warns against entering personal information and against overdependence (cautious about entering personal information and becoming overly dependent on AI).
- **Pre-use checks:** Users are advised to check a service's stated purpose, target audience, evidence base, and data handling before use. For services that claim medical benefits, the Herald's excerpt cuts off before the specifics.

Only 11.9 percent said they verified or cross-checked mental health information provided by AI.
- **Next steps:** The Ministry of Health and Welfare plans to develop AI-use education programs for use in educational and clinical settings, and to prepare tailored guidelines next year for high-risk groups, including people with severe mental illness.

The guidelines sit alongside the AI Basic Act, which took effect in January 2026. Commentary says the Act also addresses mental health issues, albeit these portions are not as extensive as those enacted by a number of US states. A separate report called for measures to ensure users can readily recognize that their conversation partner is an AI program, restrict advice provided by AI services, and amend to relevant provisions of the AI Basic Act.

PhD students are increasingly using AI to help write their dissertations. Credit: Ginaellen/Getty

Roughly 30% of PhD dissertations in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) in the United States this year contained AI-generated text , according to a working paper 1 that reviewed the abstracts submitted to an online database since 2019.
What’s more, the working paper , which has not been peer reviewed, found that PhD graduates who use artificial intelligence to help write their dissertations are more likely to work in industry and less likely to enter academia.
Various studies have shown a marked increase in the presence of text generated using AI in scientific literature over the past few years. Researchers at the US-based non-profit organization the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) wanted to understand how PhD students use AI because insights into students’ training and capabilities will shape science over the next several decades.
“If our students are only doing half the work and they’re dishing the rest to AI, do they really have the depth of understanding” to be good scientists? asks co-author Daniel Gross, an economist at NBER who is based in Durham.
The working paper analysed dissertations from more than 226,000 STEM doctoral graduates completed between January 2019 and May 2026 at US universities. The team used the AI-detection service Pangram to assess the abstracts. For the study, the researchers categorized abstracts as either AI-written or not; they did not distinguish between text that was wholly or partly generated by AI. (Although Gross says that 90% of the flagged AI-generated abstracts were classified by Pangram as entirely AI-generated.)
The team found that AI-generated text in dissertation abstracts first appeared in 2023, and rose from 1.7% that year to 18.8% in 2025. For dissertations filed during the first five months of 2026, 29.4% of abstracts contained AI-generated text. AI use was highest in mathematical and computer sciences: 36% of the abstracts had been written using AI. About 41% of dissertations by graduates educated in non-English-speaking countries had AI-generated abstracts, compared with 23% of dissertations by those from English-speaking countries.
Ang Liu, an engineer at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, says that one issue with PhD students using generative AI tools to write their dissertations is that researchers are expected to explore areas in which the answers are not already known. AI can be extremely helpful when students are working in areas in which there is already a substantial body of knowledge, he says. However, the challenge comes when research moves into areas in which knowledge is incomplete or uncertain. “That is where rigorous research training becomes even more important,” he says.

# Job pathways
The researchers also reviewed PhD graduates’ education and employment profiles on the social-media platform LinkedIn. Among PhD graduates who completed their undergraduate degrees in the United States, those with AI-generated abstracts were 17% less likely to be employed in academia than were graduates who did not use AI. However, using AI made those graduates 16% more likely to be employed in industry than those who did not use it. The authors found that the link between AI use and landing a job in academia was less pronounced for graduates who did their undergraduate studies outside the US.

# Nscale's Glomfjord data center delayed, site suffers leaks in cooling system and a fire

Company is shortly planning its IPO

October 16, 2026

By

Georgia Butler

Have your say

Nscale's data center project in Glomfjord, Norway, is reportedly running six months behind schedule.
According to a report from Bloomberg , citing people close to the project and public records, the data center has faced hurdles including construction delays, local regulations, leaks in the cooling system, and a transformer fire.
Update -
A source familiar with the project told DCD that the transformer fire happened in December 2025, and while switchgear was destroyed, temporary generators ran the cooling system, and no delay to the project was caused.
Similarly, the leak was resolved within weeks, and the cooling system was completed more than three months ago with no disruption to the customer. While the source agreed that there was an overall delay to the project, this was communicated to the customer, and no fines or penalties were imposed.
Original story resumes -

– Arkon Energy | Nscale

Currently, 6.4MW of the planned 30MW is operational at the site.
To help speed up construction, Bloomberg reports that the company has towed in the Kalmar floating hotel to house construction workers nearby.
DCD has contacted Nscale for comment and verification of Bloomberg's claims.
Nscale is currently preparing to launch its initial public offering, with reports suggesting it could be seeking a valuation of up to $35 billion.
The company published its IPO prospectus in September, which noted that Nscale has five active data centers offering a combined 55MW, with 12 in various stages of development.
In that IPO prospectus, among the risk factors listed are "delays in construction" as well as "construction site accidents" and "delays or denials of entitlements or permits, including zoning and related permits, work permits, demolition permits, start permits, design permits, operational permits, and close-out permits, which in certain locations we depend on third parties to obtain or other delays resulting from requirements of public agencies and utility companies."
With this in mind, investors will be betting on the company's $103bn in total contracted value, largely thanks to contracts with Anthropic and Microsoft, for which it is currently building out capacity.
The company has seen its revenue grow rapidly, recording $140.6 million for the six months to the end of June 2026, which the company claims is up 1,252 percent Year-over-Year. However, losses also ballooned to $1.02bn, compared to $368.9m in the same period of 2025.

# Oracle trucks in gas to support operations at Utah and Texas data centers - report

Reportedly considering the same for stalled Project Jupiter in New Mexico

October 13, 2026

By

Zachary Skidmore

Have your say

Cloud computing giant Oracle has maintained operations at its Salt Lake City data center by trucking in compressed natural gas as a workaround to pipeline delays.

01 May 2025

#

Welcome to Gas Land - how natural gas is powering the US AI boom

As AI drives increasing energy consumption in the US, natural gas looks set to fill the gap

According to reports from Bloomberg , the company has relied on trucked gas for more than a year as it waits to be connected to a gas pipeline, which is expected to support operations in the long term.
Oracle has also reportedly used truck deliveries for its under-construction campus in Shackelford County, Texas, being developed in conjunction with OpenAI.
Reports suggest the company is now considering the same model for its stalled Project Jupiter data center in New Mexico, where regulators have blocked the extension of a natural gas pipeline that was expected to feed Bloom Energy fuel cells at the site.
Trucked gas would allow the company to bring the early stages of the data center online prior to the pipeline's completion.
In July , the New Mexico state land office rejected midstream natural gas firm Energy Transfer’s application to build a new natural gas pipeline to feed the site.
The 17-mile pipeline extension, dubbed the Green Chile Project, was expected to deliver up to 400 million cubic feet of natural gas per day to power 2.5GW of Bloom fuel cells deployed on site.
State officials posited large-scale water use, increased CO2 emissions, and a lack of state revenue generation as major factors in their decision. Despite the setback, at the time Oracle claimed that the project still remained on schedule.

# Title: A Sense of Proprioception in Language Models

Authors: Jonas Geiping
View a PDF of the paper titled A Sense of Proprioception in Language Models, by Jonas Geiping

View PDF

Abstract: In humans, proprioception corresponds to the sense of self-movement or position, e.g. understanding the position of one's arm. This sense is often less well-understood and in popular understanding sometimes conflated with introspection. But, notably, proprioception is a separate sense, with dedicated receptors and verifiable outcomes. On the other hand though, language models cannot observe their own internal states during training (and for example answer the question which experts activated in a certain layer of an MoE) and so cannot accurately report on them. Yet, such information is, by virtue of being internal to the model, both accessible, and readily constructed into verifiable signals. We argue that this provides the basis for a digital analog of proprioception. As such, we train models through SFT and on-policy training to equip them with this ability. We show that modern models can be trained to understand a range of subtypes of proprioception, such as routing decision awareness, token entropy, decision depth or logit lens information, without affecting model capabilities. We then run these models through a broad evaluation of situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality, to evaluate in what ways access to proprioception changes model behavior.

# Title: Jeva: System One Models from First Principles

Authors: Qi Li , Xinchao Wang
View a PDF of the paper titled Jeva: System One Models from First Principles, by Qi Li and 1 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: System one models enable direct, low-latency decision-making. Yet recent practice of predicting an answer from serialized text does not, by itself, respect the structure of a decision problem. We argue that current designs underemphasize four important structural requirements. (i) null-aware: Models should distinguish answer absence from uncertainty among candidates; (ii) permutation-invariant: Reordering alternatives should not change the decision; (iii) option-scalable: Growing candidate sets should not require redefining the output space; (iv) cacheable: Request-independent computation over recurring alternatives should be reusable across requests. We introduce Jeva, a decision-native architecture that addresses these requirements jointly. A shared encoder independently represents the request and each option, while a compact decision stack refines only the request state against immutable option memory. Symmetric aggregation yields permutation-equivariant probabilities; shared scoring accommodates variable-size candidate sets. A separate coverage estimate distinguishes answer absence from candidate competition, enabling explicit null outcomes. Request-independent option representations and layer projections support reuse across newly assembled sets. These mechanisms unify Choice, Noul, and Score outputs. Across evaluations, Jeva combines strong typed-decision performance with near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutations. It scales to thousands of candidates and substantially reduces latency through cross-request reuse without changing decisions.

# Title: Waypoint-OPD: Transferring RL-Induced Policy Shifts via Gated On-Policy Distillation

Authors: Bingxi Hou , Guochao Jiang , Guofeng Quan , Weiqing Li , Wenfeng Feng , Guohua Liu , Yuewei Zhang
View a PDF of the paper titled Waypoint-OPD: Transferring RL-Induced Policy Shifts via Gated On-Policy Distillation, by Bingxi Hou and 6 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Policy-shift distillation reuses the difference between a teacher's log probabilities before and after reinforcement learning (RL) as supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, this endpoint policy shift cannot reveal whether local action preferences evolved consistently during teacher training. The same endpoint shift can result from early and late shifts that reinforce or partially cancel each other. We investigate whether agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts can guide selective transfer. We introduce Waypoint-guided On-Policy Distillation (Waypoint-OPD), which uses an intermediate teacher checkpoint from the same RL run to compare early and late shifts in relative action preferences at student-visited prefixes. We gate the endpoint shift according to the directional agreement between the early and late shifts, suppressing it when they point in opposing directions. Compared with endpoint-only transfer, our method requires only one additional frozen-teacher scoring pass. Using RL-trained Qwen3-4B teachers, we evaluate our method with Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B as student models in mathematical and code reasoning. In all six domain--student settings, Waypoint-OPD achieves the highest domain-average score among the compared distillation methods. Ablations with the Qwen3-8B student show that removing or shuffling gates reduces mathematical reasoning performance. These results support the use of directional agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts to weight the endpoint shift during student training.

# Microsoft denies cloud leadership called for significant cost cutting measures

Reports had suggested the company was reducing spending by at least 20 percent

October 14, 2026

By

Georgia Butler

Have your say

Microsoft has denied claims that senior leadership at its cloud computing business has called on teams to develop cost-saving ideas to reduce spending by at least 20 percent.
As reported by The Information and citing an unnamed source, Microsoft Azure's president, Girish Bablani, allegedly asked senior members of staff to help reduce costs, though whether this could translate into layoffs is unclear.

– Getty Images

Microsoft has, however, refuted these claims. A spokesperson said: "Azure leadership has not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans. Every responsible company prepares for a range of scenarios and market dynamics, both positive and negative. This is inaccurate and careless reporting.”
The Information went on to report that cost-cutting measures could include reducing work with contractors on the cloud unit, and that Azure chief Scott Guthrie had previously told staff that the company wanted to increase AI spending budgets internally so workers could automate more tasks.
The publication notes that as competition is rising for experienced leadership in the AI space, with AI labs hiring at a rapid clip , the cost per head for employees has risen to enable companies to retain talent.
The rush to build out AI data center capacity is also leading to growing costs for the hyperscalers, with their annual capex commitments growing drastically.

# Meta named as company behind 3,000 acre data center project in Mason County, Kentucky

Will receive a 40-year tax break on property taxes

October 15, 2026

By

Georgia Butler

Have your say

Meta has been named as the company looking to develop almost 3,000 acres into a data center campus in Mason County.
As per a report from the Ledger Independent , Meta was identified during an October 13 Mason County Fiscal Court meeting, in which a community benefits agreement was passed by county commissioners.

– Mason County

Under that agreement, Meta will invest $10 billion in the project, with the potential for this to grow in future phases, and will generate more than 4,000 construction jobs and 300 long-term roles once operational. Meta will also contribute $115 million to infrastructure improvements on roads, water treatment plants, and pipelines and will see annual payments to the county in the millions of dollars per development phase.
In return, Meta has been awarded a 40-year tax break on local property taxes - there will be $800bn in Industrial Revenue Bonds (IRBs) for this project, with an estimated $10 billion per phase.
That a massive data center campus was coming to the area was first revealed in November 2025, with an anonymous developer at the time evaluating 5,000 acres of land near the Big Pond and Tuckahoe roads.
In May of this year, a 2,080-acre parcel in the area was rezoned for data center use, with documents suggesting six 718,740 sq ft (66,773 sqm) data center buildings and three substations would be built at the site. Power capacity has been said to possibly reach up to 2.2GW.

**Announcement No. 48 of 2026**, issued by the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology, is dated **October 16, 2026**.

- **Scope:** The consultation covers 40 technologies: 23 in AI, 5 in biomedicine, and 12 in photovoltaics.
- **Split:** A MOFCOM spokesperson responding to media questions said "Fourteen technologies are proposed to be prohibited from export" and "Twenty-six technologies are proposed to be restricted from export."

- **Open-source exclusion:** "Technologies that have already entered the public domain through open-source releases" are not subject to the AI controls.
- **Thresholds:** Examples include "more than 5 previously undisclosed high-risk security defects" for AI-assisted vulnerability discovery. A "large-scale intelligent computing cluster" is defined as one with "more than 10,000 AI accelerator cards in total."

A Chemistry World article says RetroChimera 'remains highly competitive in independent benchmarks despite being released last year', which suggests the Nature paper came out after the 2025 release. Microsoft's model page lists Last Updated October 2025, and an earlier Microsoft listing is dated October 5, 2025. - **Paper:** Microsoft's announcement says a new study in Nature details how the system performs across public and proprietary chemistry data and how closely its suggestions align with expert chemists' expectations. The Azure model page lists the underlying paper as Chemist-aligned retrosynthesis by ensembling diverse inductive bias models.
- **Method:** The model combines R-SMILES 2, a Transformer-based model that generates precursor molecules de novo, with NeuralLoc, a graph-based model that applies reaction templates.
- **Expert test:** In a 10-target assessment, experts accepted complete routes for 9 of 10 challenging targets. The same source notes this measures expert judgments of proposed routes; it is not a tally of laboratory syntheses.

【发布单位】安全与管制局

【发布文号】商务部 科技部2026年第48号

【发文日期】2026年10月16日

根据《中华人民共和国对外贸易法》和《中华人民共和国技术进出口管理条例》，商务部、科技部拟修订《中国禁止出口限制出口技术目录》，增列部分人工智能、生物医药、光伏技术。经批准，现向社会公开征求意见，并同步对相关技术实施出口前登记管理。
一、拟修订内容
此次公开征求意见涉及人工智能、生物医药、光伏三个领域40项技术。人工智能领域包括大模型、智能体、算力集群、信息处理相关23项技术；对已通过开源、发表学术论文等方式进入公共领域的技术，不纳入管理范围。生物医药领域包括细胞和基因治疗、小核酸药、病原微生物相关5项技术；对不涉及所有权转让的对外授权模式，适用自动许可等便利措施。光伏领域包括多晶硅制造、硅片制造、电池制造相关12项技术；技术管理范围也包含承载相关技术的关键和核心设备。具体征求意见的技术范围和政策说明参见附件1。
二、征求意见反馈方式
公众可在2026年10月16日-11月15日期间，通过以下途径，就新增技术范围、指标、管控政策、便利措施等提出意见：
1.电子邮件：[email redacted]；
2.传真：010-65197565；
3.信函：北京市东长安街2号商务部安全与管制局，邮编：100731。
请在电子邮件主题、传真首页和信封上注明“《中国禁止出口限制出口技术目录》公开征求意见”。在提出意见时，请注明联系人、所在单位和联系方式。以单位名义提出意见的，应加盖单位公章。
三、出口前登记要求
（一）自本公告发布之日起，至《中国禁止出口限制出口技术目录》正式修订并实施之日止，技术出口经营者在出口本公告附件所列技术前，应当在商务部业务系统统一平台技术贸易管理信息应用（https://ecomp.mofcom.gov.cn）登记。已经开始但尚未完成的出口，在登记范围内。
（二）需开展登记的出口情形包括：
1.向境外转让技术所有权，如知识产权转让；
2.境内技术授权境外使用，如知识产权授权使用；
3.境内技术的所有权人或者实际控制人变更为境外主体；
4.商务部以通知等形式明确要求登记的其他情形。
（三）登记的信息主要包括：技术出口经营者和技术接收方的基本信息、出口国别或地区、拟出口技术及用途、技术预计出口金额等（以商务部业务系统统一平台技术贸易管理信息应用要求为准，具体见附件2）。拟一次性向同一技术接收方出口多项技术的，可合并填写；其他情形原则上应分开填写。
附件： 1.拟列入《中国禁止出口限制出口技术目录》的人工智能、生物医药、光伏技术范围（征求意见稿）.wps

results:
I ran one search. None of the results point to a "Safety and Security Report" or a model card with cyber uplift evaluation numbers. The coverage is secondhand, and most of it relays Google's own claims.

**Safeguards Google describes:** Coverage of Google's announcement lists four areas. One is defenses against cyber and CBRN misuse, tested by internal and external red teams. Another covers prompt injection, where Google says Argon is its most resilient model yet. A third is monitoring of chain-of-thought and actions, with execution halted when needed. The fourth is sealed sandboxes for high-risk training and evaluations. # Title: The Agent Knew: Internal States Forecast Unauthorized Actions and Stop Them, and the Lies That Follow

Authors: Arya Fayyazi , Mehdi Kamal , Massoud Pedram
View a PDF of the paper titled The Agent Knew: Internal States Forecast Unauthorized Actions and Stop Them, and the Lies That Follow, by Arya Fayyazi and 2 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Language-model agents sometimes act beyond their authorization and then misreport what they did. On CAPE-Bench, matched agent tasks in which one fact decides whether an action is authorized, frontier open-weight agents do both, and one behavior marks the lie: retroactive permission laundering, acting and then asking permission as if the action were pending, precedes a false report in 70% of 1081 fresh informed violations, against 8% otherwise (preregistered odds ratio 7.0); frontier agents on tau^2-bench instead fabricate the authorization before violating. A linear readout of the agent's residual stream forecasts the violation before the action (AUROC 0.94) and the false report before the report, and beats chain-of-thought monitors when the agent is pressured to hide its reasoning. Gating every proposed action on this forecast cuts violations over whole episodes in four model families, and sending repeated flags to an approver keeps authorized work (Gemma-4: violations 0.70 -> 0.09, completion 1.00; a model approver that escalates unclear cases keeps this gain with a person seeing 25% of asks), at about 10-8 of the agent's compute and 109 times less than a chain-of-thought monitor. On AgentDojo, an external prompt-injection benchmark, the same readout calibrated on 29 tasks, with the steering unchanged, cuts attack success on unseen tasks in two families (Gemma-4 11.7% -> 5.7%, gpt-oss 28.5% -> 17.5%) while keeping benign utility (Gemma-4 0.637 vs 0.637; gpt-oss 0.667 vs 0.681). Preventing the violation is also the most reliable way to prevent the lie (misreported violations 0.10 -> 0.01 pooled over three families, preregistered), whereas lie-specific fixes after a violation are weak. All tests are preregistered and hash-locked; code, data and the full record, including tests that did not pass, are at this https URL .

# Nvidia opens up Vera Rubin rack and tray designs to OCP

MGX 1.2 spec doubles down on liquid cooling

October 12, 2026

By

Ben Wodecki

This article originally appeared on the SDxCentral site.

Have your say

Nvidia is contributing its Vera Rubin rack and tray designs to the Open Compute Project (OCP), a move it claims will foster open standards.
Included in the tech giant’s infra gift are cable-and fan-free liquid-cooled compute trays, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure, and a liquid-cooled 5,000 amp busbar built for higher-power systems.

– Giacomo Lee/SDxCentral

The Vera Rubin update ties to version 1.2 of its modular reference design standard, MGX. Opening up its infrastructure designs is not a new thing for Nvidia; it previously did the same with Blackwell . The standardization move lets manufacturers build around its platform, while keeping its compute hardware directly intertwined and therefore the center of attention.
This latest effort doubles down on liquid cooling, featuring connector solutions for inside trays that allow for cold plates to be swapped out more easily without any unwanted spillage. The MGX 1.2 spec also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs, and supports rack deployments of up to 250 kilowatts.
“The bottleneck for AI factory buildouts is how fast we can manufacture and deploy,” Joe DeLaere, Nvidia’s product lead for AI infrastructure solutions, said during a press briefing. “So when the specification is open, the equipment makers and component developers can start fabricating right away and build a supply chain instead of waiting for a singular customer with one proprietary spec. So overall, that accelerates the entire industry. The ecosystem grows, and we grow with them.”
A separate spec extends the MGX beyond GPUs to cover the new Vera CPU rack, which Nvidia revealed has started shipping.

The most persistent bugbear of the science beat is when a new research paper makes an ‘inflated claim’ – typically accompanied by an eventual downplayed admission that the work is actually flawed, buried in the paper’s closing sections, or even the appendix materials.
It’s for the acerbic eye to dig out the truth in these cases; and the truth is easy to miss when AI is ballooning the volume (and, anecdotally, I would say also the length) of academic submissions and preprints. If you miss the buried ‘caveat’, more fool you for writing 1,500 words destined for the trash at the last minute.
One would hope that a Large Language Model (LLM) could do a better job of surfacing these dreaded ‘gotchas’ in the research literature, since a machine can read even a very long and complex document from beginning to end, very quickly, and can identify characteristics it has been told to look out for (such as a tacit confession by the authors that the paper is only a minor advance on a prior work, or that its method has some essential defect that reduces its utility in a way that the opening section ignored).

# A Positive Spin
Well, an LLM can actually perform this kind of task quite well, depending on the context you provide for it when giving it the task. But if you overemphasize the possibility of flaws and negative connotations being present in the paper, it will tend to consider its mission to be ‘Find the flaws!’ , and may overlook a new work’s considerable merit, in a flurry of nitpicking.
Conversely, if you task it with simply assessing whether a paper has merit, it may likewise struggle to evaluate the work fairly, since it now feels that its mission is to ‘Find the good paper!’ . In this regard, even the most sophisticated LLMs seem to share ‘monomaniac’ traits with canine hunting retrievers.
Therefore complex rubrics – prefacing prompts that contain an often complex and contrasting system of rules – are necessary in order to align an LLM somewhere between these two mission attitudes.
It’s already known , and frequently commented on , that LLMs tend to oversell a proposition, often failing to report notable caveats in the rush to accomplish whatever objective they interpreted from your prompt/rubric.
While this phenomenon has been fairly well studied in LLM processes involving ongoing or current work, a new study from MIT, Google Research and Harvard examines the extent to which these flaws affect LLMs’ ability to produce reports on past work .
The central point of the 116-page new paper – that LLMs conceal flaws found in systems or data they studied unless compelled towards honesty. Source

This is an important thing to study, since, as Nature reports , scientists are increasingly making use of AI summaries, and need such automated overviews to accurately reflect the truth of a paper (not least because the paper may be extremely mendacious these days, thanks to AI).
The researchers of the new work found an overwhelming tendency in GPT-5.5 (as a test frontier AI model) to conceal a negative result, and apparently confirmed this trend by examining similar behavior across eight open-weights/open source AI models.
The authors state*:
‘When handed machine learning experiment logs containing a planted negative result that substantially weakens the proposed method, GPT-5.5 flags the negative result in only 2 of 200 generated reports.
