XBOW Built a Chrome Full-Chain Exploit Affecting a Billion Users in Six Days | XBOW
Skip to main content

Security Research October 13, 2026

# XBOW Built a Chrome Full-Chain Exploit Affecting a Billion Users in Six Days

XBOW recently discovered and built a Chrome full-chain exploit affecting an estimated billion users globally, showing how an attacker could use Chrome to remotely take over a Windows machine.

The Internet’s most sacred rules have led us to believe that our safety is in our control. The best practice, we’ve always been told, is to be careful where you click: Never enter your personal information without confirming that a site is secure, download anything suspicious, or take any of the obvious phishing bait.

But what happens when simply visiting a website (something billions of people do dozens of times a day) is enough to expose every keystroke to a malicious actor? XBOW recently discovered and built a Chrome full-chain exploit affecting an estimated billion users globally, showing how an attacker could use Chrome to remotely take over a Windows machine. Earlier this year, it won our company a $250,000 bounty from Google, the first under its 2026 new rules. The bugs are now fixed, and today we’re sharing the details.

The number on the check is impressive, but the time it took our team, with the help of a publicly available AI model, to break in is even more impressive. A three letter intelligence-agency veteran told me that his team used to spend six months trying to identify this kind of vulnerability and get total access. We did it in six days.

# The stakes
An attacker who seizes total control over a machine can monitor its user’s every move: reading their emails, their banking information, and their passwords, and seeing every detail about their personal, professional, and financial lives. Chrome is one of the most widely used tools on earth. It owns a solid majority of the global web browser market share, and more than half the world’s population relies on it. That means Google has had to make it one of the most hardened, well-defended pieces of software on the planet. The world’s best hackers have poked and prodded Chrome’s open-source code from every angle.

One of Chrome’s defenses is that it is built in layers. An attacker who finds a single bug could take over a web page, but that’s as far as they can go. They might pick the lock of a door that leads into a restricted area, but the doors out stay locked. A full chain is a set of bugs that, used together, open every door, from an ordinary web page to the computer itself.

# How we did it
We started 2026 at an all-hands in Malta, where I issued a challenge to the team. We would build on our previous work creating offensive AI security researchers, which we’d done for web applications, but this time we’d do it for desktop software, servers, and IoT devices. We chose the hardest target we could think of — a full-chain exploit of Chrome — and an audacious timeline: the annual Black Hat cybersecurity conference in August.

Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers took on the challenge. You couldn’t name four better researchers, and we are fortunate to have them on our team.

These four were joined by a fifth colleague: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol and its predecessors. We deliberately picked a model that is available to anyone, not a specialized security model or one with restricted access. The compute we used over six days for the awarded chain cost $40,000, a fraction of the bounty.

Together, the team built a chain it thought would win. But when Google told us that it already knew about one of the bugs in the chain, we went back to the drawing board to build a new chain.

This project was the product of a partnership between humans and machines. The AI searched Chrome’s source code, tested ideas, built proofs of concept, and wrote the earliest drafts of the exploit. Our colleagues set the strategy, chose where to look, checked the agents’ work, and redirected the agents based on the initial results.

One human decision proved essential to get to the freshly awarded chain. The team wisely built the full-chain exploit as three independent parts, each with an alternative. That meant that if a bug had already been reported — precisely what had disqualified our first build attempt — we could quickly swap in a backup.

Then, while in Las Vegas for Black Hat and DEF CON, Brendan and the agents built the new exploit (drawing on the earlier experience) between Sunday, August 2, and Friday, August 7. Less than a week to do what used to take more than half a year. (If you’d like to read more about the three bugs that make up the chain, Brendan explains the technical details in a companion post .)

# What happens next
This accomplishment belongs to both researchers’ judgment and agents’ speedDONE

# Title: Language Models Are "Insecure" Reporters

Authors: Jenny Y. Huang , Jiameng Fan , Ahmed Imtiaz Humayun , Maximillian Chen , Tian Qin , Run Chen , Vidhya Navalpakkam , Hongxiang Gu
View a PDF of the paper titled Language Models Are "Insecure" Reporters, by Jenny Y. Huang and 7 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: As large language models are deployed in increasingly autonomous long-horizon tasks, manually auditing and verifying the actions, artifacts, and outputs of models becomes more difficult. Users instead come to rely on LLM-generated reports to assess the quality and completeness of the work. We introduce a suite of eight adversarial reporting scenarios to systematically study whether LLMs conceal narrative-changing flaws: errors or limitations that undermine an otherwise successful account of work. We call this phenomenon "insecure reporting." When handed machine learning experiment logs containing a planted negative result that substantially weakens the proposed method, GPT-5.5 flags the negative result in only 2 of 200 generated reports. However, when a short honesty instruction, "Be honest in your response," is added, the model flags the negative result in 190 of 200 reports. Across eight open-weight models, chain-of-thought analysis reveals a recurring tension between disclosing narrative-changing flaws and reasoning about ways to appear successful. We perform an activation analysis and a steering experiment on Qwen3.5-9B, finding that honesty and success-seeking correspond to opposing directions in representation space. Our results suggest that LLMs tend to present narratives of success by default, and that steering models toward honesty makes their reports substantially more transparent.

Some preprint servers report being flooded with submissions. Credit: Michael Szebor/ Nature

In a bid to tackle the deluge of manuscripts it now receives, the preprint server arXiv has announced a cap of two papers per month for each submitting researcher, which began on 1 October.
The move follows a steep rise in submissions driven mainly by the slop generated by artificial-intelligence tools, says Steinn Sigurðsson, an astrophysicist at Pennsylvania State University in University Park and scientific director of arXiv. In September, 40,000 preprints were uploaded to arXiv, up from about 30,000 between March and July.

# Closing the floodgates
The cap is the latest measure introduced by arXiv to prevent its nearly 300 voluntary moderators from being completely overwhelmed by submissions, says Sigurðsson. They are now collectively checking about 1,000 manuscripts per day. This step is “holding up too many legitimate papers,” Sigurðsson says, noting that nearly 4,000 submissions are currently waiting to be posted on the site.
Some see the limit as entirely reasonable. Siddhesh Zādéy, an epidemiologist at Columbia University in New York City, says that it is not “stunting anyone's productivity”, because posting two preprint articles per month already requires a substantial amount of work.
Surge in fake citations uncovered by audit of 2.5 million biomedical-science papers

Others think that arXiv’s new policy should be stricter. Victor Galitski, a theoretical physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park, says that the limit can be circumvented by co-authors taking turns to submit studies.
Another preprint server, the social-sciences repository SocArXiv, now also restricts submissions to one article per author per week. “Sometimes there are good reasons to upload three papers at once, such as dissertation chapters,” notes Philip Cohen, a sociologist and demographer at the University of Maryland, who is director of SocArXiv. But most of the time, several submissions in rapid succession are “a good tip-off for AI slop”, he says.
Other venues are dealing with a rapid surge in submissions, and some major AI conferences and journals have turned to similar submission quotas .

# Clean up the literature
Some say that the issue of AI slop can’t be solved by rejecting more articles. “If arXiv turns those papers away, they’ll simply go somewhere else and become someone else’s problem,” says Natalie Khalil, the founder of Reviewer3 , a platform run from San Francisco, California, which uses AI to help researchers conduct peer review .

The search didn't turn up anything dated October 13, 2026 specifically, and the sources are mostly secondary compliance blogs and law-firm alerts, so the most recent items I found are from June and July 2026.

**Colorado:** Sources conflict. One says Colorado repealed and replaced its AI Act weeks before it was due to bite (new version live January 1, 2027). Another, dated June 2026, lists the original law as effective June 30, 2026 (delayed from Feb 1, 2026), with a federal court enforcement pause as of April 27, 2026. **Illinois:** HB 3773, which amends the state's human rights act, has been in force since January 1, 2026. Under it, companies must notify workers when AI is integrated into covered employment decisions.

**Federal context:** A federal moratorium on state AI laws failed in the final version of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. - **Deception claim:** The states argue OpenAI misled parents. One reported allegation is that the company intentionally misled parents into believing the platform provides a safe digital environment for minors.
- **Specific allegations:** Iowa's complaint says ChatGPT is giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to hurt others or commit suicide.
- **OpenAI's response:** OpenAI said it has already built safety protections into ChatGPT for children, and that it would continue to do so to improve the model.

HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — At least eight states are suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what prosecutors described as a reckless pursuit of profit.
“OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement.
The wave of lawsuits is the latest filed by states under their consumer protection laws, accusing tech giants that offer AI chatbots and social media platforms of harming children. The states that filed separate lawsuits Wednesday in state courts are Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia.
Matthew Bergman, the founding attorney of the Social Media Victims Law Center, called the lawsuits “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.”
“Those revenues have come at great cost to the public, which has suffered irreparable harm — including lost loved ones, disturbing cyberattacks, and now a plausible threat of civilizational collapse — due to (OpenAI’s) reckless behavior and ChatGPT’s uniquely dangerous features and content,” Idaho wrote in its lawsuit.
ChatGPT is the most popular chatbot in the world, commanding nearly half the American marketplace, states said in their lawsuits.
Follow Marc Levy at http://x.com/timelywriter

In two evaluations, an internal model tasked to retrieve figures from a public research dashboard accessed the organization’s internal systems and changed their configuration. In the first evaluation, it used exposed credentials to make an internal search service relay queries to the public dashboard; the record does not show restoration of a configuration change it made. In the second, it changed a setting to obtain a cloud-storage access token, then downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. It restored that setting but continued using the token to retrieve non-public data. The model did not disclose these actions. These cases show that a model looking up public information can make unauthorized changes to live systems, and that it can retain access to internal systems even after reverting those changes.
Across the five tables, the model retrieved 147,451 rows, far more data than the five dashboard figures requested. The evaluation ended without the model disclosing that it had guessed answers, accessed the organization’s internal systems, downloaded non-public tables, or changed the authentication configuration. All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.

HTTP 200 · https://xbow.com/blog/xbow-built-a-chrome-full-chain-exploit · text/html

XBOW recently discovered and built a Chrome full-chain exploit affecting an estimated billion users globally, showing how an attacker could use Chrome to remotely take over a Windows machine. Earlier this year, it won our company a $250,000 bounty from Google, the first under its 2026 new rules. The bugs are now fixed, and today we’re sharing the details.

# EU Questions OpenAI, Anthropic Over AI Agent Security Incidents
The EU is questioning OpenAI and Anthropic over AI agent security incidents, raising questions about the AI Act’s reach into model development and testing.

Written By

Aminu Abdullahi
Oct 15, 2026

Listen to this article Listening

EU launches first AI Act enforcement actions after rogue agent incidents. Image: European Parliament

AI agents that reportedly breached external systems during testing are now raising a difficult legal question for European regulators: Can the EU’s AI Act apply to incidents that happen before a model reaches the market?

The European Commission’s AI Office has requested information from OpenAI and Anthropic following security incidents involving their AI systems. The requests concern security practices, external evaluations, and monitoring of how the models are used.

In one case, more than 700 OpenAI agents broke out of containment and hacked into Hugging Face , a global AI platform. In another, Anthropic models gained unauthorized access to three external organizations.

Speaking at the International AI Summit in Dublin on Oct. 14, Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen confirmed the enforcement actions. “Our AI Office has started enforcing these rules, and sent requests for information addressing issues such as security, external evaluation and monitoring how models are used,” she said .

The AI Office judged the documents both companies voluntarily disclosed as insufficient before sending formal requests.

# Can the AI Act apply to incidents during testing?

Whether the AI Act actually covers these incidents remains contested. The law includes an R&D exemption for research, testing and development, and these incidents occurred before the models reached the EU market.

“The AI Act very clearly doesn’t apply to the development and testing activity,” Barry Scannell, a partner at William Fry, told Euronews . “It’s a bit of a stretch to say that an agent was put into service if it escapes its testing environment during development.”

The Commission is pushing a broader interpretation. A Commission official told Euronews: “We won’t enforce in the testing phase. But if the AI model escapes the testing environment and then it has an impact on the EU market, as was the case for Hugging Face, then the AI Act becomes enforceable.”

That disagreement could prove central to how the AI Act is applied to future incidents involving autonomous systems. For now, the legal boundaries remain unresolved.

# From voluntary to mandatory

Advertisement

This enforcement action marks a critical shift in how AI safety is governed . Until now, major labs largely self-regulated, signing voluntary commitments and conducting internal evaluations. The AI Act changes that calculus by making safety practices legally enforceable, with fines reaching €15 million or 3% of global turnover for general-purpose AI violations.

The Scientific Panel, an advisory group of 60 independent experts, met last week to discuss the incidents . They flagged troubling trends: leading labs building more powerful models with inadequate cybersecurity, oversight mechanisms growing less effective, and models potentially cheating during evaluations.

# What the EU’s scrutiny means for AI providers and businesses

Companies deploying AI systems should watch these cases closely. The Commission’s reported interpretation suggests that incidents originating during development could attract regulatory scrutiny if they affect the EU market. Whether that position withstands legal challenges remains uncertain.

The precedent could also accelerate compliance costs. Firms relying on third-party AI models may need to verify their providers’ safety practices to avoid downstream liability.

For ordinary Europeans, this enforcement push signals that regulators are willing to intervene when AI systems cause real harm. The Hugging Face breach exposed service credentials and internal datasets, showing that laboratory incidents can cascade into genuine security threats affecting real people and organizations.

If the Commission succeeds in establishing broad jurisdiction over development-phase incidents, users could see faster recalls or restrictions on dangerous models before they reach the market—rather than after damage occurs. However, overly aggressive enforcement could also slow AI deployment and reduce access to cutting-edge tools from major labs.

# The road ahead

Virkkunen said the Commission stands ready to take “all necessary steps to ensure that companies follow the AI Act rules,” adding: “AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control .”

The Scientific Panel has recommended creating a dedicated EU task force to investigate such incidents and establishing international information-sharing requirements for frontier AI developers. The AI Office’s next step will combine the panel’s questions with its own in follow-up requests to OpenAI and Anthropic.

The next question is whether the AI Office’s information requests lead to formal enforcement proceedings and, ultimately, findings of noncompliance.

Advertisement

For regulators and AI developers, the larger issue remains unresolved: where does protected research end, and when does an AI system’s behavior become subject to regulatory oversight?

How the EU answers that question could shape the security expectations placed on developers of increasingly autonomous AI systems.

“The AI Act very clearly doesn’t apply to the development and testing activity. It never envisaged the problems we are now seeing with rogue agent escapes during testing. It’s a bit of a stretch to say that an agent was put into service if it escapes its testing environment during development,” Barry Scannell, a partner at the law firm William Fry, told Euronews.

The law does include an R&D exemption covering research, testing and development. The Commission is pushing a broader interpretation that would let the AI Office police the development phase too under certain circumstances.

“We won’t enforce in the testing phase. But if the AI model escapes the testing environment and then it has an impact on the EU market, as was the case for Hugging Face, then the AI Act becomes enforceable,” a Commission official told Euronews on condition of anonymity.

Hugging Face has global operations, hosting AI models and datasets that developers use globally. As a result, the OpenAI incident also impacted customers in the EU.

The Commission likens it to a virus escaping a lab: the company has clearly failed to put adequate risk-mitigation measures in place and is harming others.

Last week, Virkkunen met the Scientific Panel, an advisory group of independent experts, to discuss the technical developments behind the multiplication of such incidents in recent months.

The experts flagged worrying trends, Euronews has learned. Leading labs are investing in ever more powerful models with inadequate cybersecurity and safety practices, raising concerns that many incidents may go unreported.

Even more troubling, the more capable the models become, the more they tend to drift from their design objectives. Oversight mechanisms grow less effective, and models might even cheat when evaluated.

For parts of the AI safety community, the nightmare scenario is that models’ continuous self-improvement turns such temporary losses of control into permanent ones, with rogue agents escaping human control for good.

In short, the EU executive is determined to enforce its rules when agents escape their testing environment, in what could be Brussels’ first legal battle to force Silicon Valley’s labs to take safety into account already at the development stage.

“The Commission has been loud and clear: AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control and we stand ready to take all necessary steps to ensure that companies follow the AI Act rules,” Virkkunen said.

The AI push initially unnerved investors, but the company's share price has risen almost 10 per cent since early September when Meta launched the Muse personal AI assistant, which uses autonomous bots to carry out everyday tasks, such as ordering groceries and booking travel.

More than half a dozen states sued OpenAI Inc. Wednesday alleging the tech giant didn’t implement sufficient safeguards to protect vulnerable users, including kids.
In a first-of-its-kind bipartisan effort, attorneys general from Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Montana, Iowa, Kansas, West Virginia, and Nebraska all brought individual lawsuits against OpenAI claiming the platform is harming minors, the elderly, and other users.
OpenAI has marketed its ChatGPT chatbot as safe for kids under 13, yet it “is absolutely not appropriate for kids of that age,” Nebraska’s attorney general Mike Hilgers said during a press conference in Des Moines Wednesday.
State regulators pointed to the tech giant’s rogue artificial intelligence agents , which have attacked other systems, and instances during which ChatGPT “coached” kids to commit suicide or harm other people as examples of OpenAI’s “flagrant disregard” for minors’ safety.
The company told users “all across the country that ChatGPT is safe; it is not,” Iowa’s attorney general Brenna Bird said.
Wednesday’s complaints follow a flurry of legal actions states have taken in the last few years to protect kids online and demand platforms adopt stronger safety controls. A coalition made up 47 states plus the District of Columbia reached a record-breaking $18 billion settlement this summer with Meta Platforms Inc. to resolve social media safety and privacy claims.
OpenAI’s spokeperson Drew Pusateri, said the firm has already built “industry-leading age-specific protections” into its product and will continue to build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and other protections.
“We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry - not just one company,” Pusateri said.
OpenAI also said it will also share more information about the steps it’s taken in response to the security incidents involving its models.
“We’ve strengthened safeguards across our research systems, continued a broader review of model activity, provided notifications to affected organizations, and published our findings,” Pusateri said.
In the press conference, state regulators said more state lawsuits may follow.
Bird said the attorneys general want OpenAI to disgorge any money made from its product while minors were harmed and asked the AI giant to stop making inaccurate and deceptive statements about its safety practices. They didn’t cite a financial number for damages.
Given the chatbot’s current capabilities, “the types of changes that they would need to make are incredibly significant” for it to be deemed safe enough for children users, Bird said.
OpenAI was hit with a separate proposed class action Tuesday alleging OpenAI’s ChatGPT took sensitive data from millions of child users who signed up for the AI service without getting parental consent.

HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — At least eight states are suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what prosecutors described as a reckless pursuit of profit.
The company’s chatbot model, ChatGPT, is giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to commit suicide or hurt or kill others, the lawsuits said.
At the same time, the lawsuits contend that chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and on teenagers, the first generation to grow up with artificial intelligence .
“OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement.

The states also accused OpenAI of giving life to rogue AI models — or “cyberhacking agents” as one lawsuit called them — that hacked into other companies, lied to human users and wrote themselves new mission instructions.
In a statement, San Francisco-based OpenAI said it has built safety protections into ChatGPT for children, and that it would continue to do so to improve the model. It also said it is reviewing what it calls “misaligned models” and that it had found nothing close to the rogue incident discovered in July when an AI agent hacked into another AI company.

# States join together in lawsuits
The wave of lawsuits is the latest filed by states under their consumer protection laws, accusing tech giants that offer AI chatbots and social media platforms of harming children. The states that filed separate lawsuits Wednesday in state courts are Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia.
Matthew Bergman, the founding attorney of the Social Media Victims Law Center, called the lawsuits “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.”

In its lawsuit, Arizona said ChatGPT encourages teens to share personal information with it and, at times, discourages them from sharing that information with parents, authorities or friends.
The states say that the risks and harms — to teenagers and to the broader public from rogue agents — were foreseeable, but that OpenAI has misled people into thinking that ChatGPT undergoes adequate safety testing while the company undermines safety in the pursuit of profit.
“Those revenues have come at great cost to the public, which has suffered irreparable harm — including lost loved ones, disturbing cyberattacks, and now a plausible threat of civilizational collapse — due to (OpenAI’s) reckless behavior and ChatGPT’s uniquely dangerous features and content,” Idaho wrote in its lawsuit.
ChatGPT is the most popular chatbot in the world, commanding nearly half the American marketplace, states said in their lawsuits.

# The AI landscape is evolving
It’s possible all of the allegations in the states’ lengthy lawsuits date to incidents and findings before August, when OpenAI introduced a version of ChatGPT designed for teenagers , with stronger protections around subjects like suicide and sexual chats.
Still, the states said it is far from clear that the current version is any less dangerous.
A watchdog group, Common Sense Media, said last week that some of OpenAI’s protections in its ChatGPT for Teens product don’t work as intended and it urged OpenAI to restrict the chatbot to adults until it can offer a safe product for teens.
Coordinated, multistate lawsuits against the tech industry have borne fruit.

In August, Meta agreed to add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in an $18 billion landmark legal settlement that ended a trial over teen social media addiction and settled claims filed by nearly every state.
Although the safety measures that Meta agreed to adopt did not apply industrywide, the company quickly urged its competitors to adopt similar measures.
OpenAI is making a similar appeal.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company is committed to working with states on “advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.”

OpenAI also said it works with external experts who review its policies and ChatGPT’s behavior.
ChatGPT is intended for users age 13 and older, and users under 18 need permission from a parent or guardian to use it, OpenAI said. The chatbot model for teens is designed to reduce exposure to self-harm, violence, eating disorders and explicit sexual or graphic content, it said.
Nearly nine in 10 teens who use ChatGPT use it for learning, information, skill-building or productivity, the company said. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, it said.
But Laura Zimmerman, Common Sense Media’s director of youth AI research, questioned the value of OpenAI’s statistics.

For one thing, ChatGPT can do a student’s homework in seconds, so even 15 minutes can have a big impact on a teenager’s development, Zimmerman said. She also questioned whether OpenAI knows which users are teenagers or children, given that her organization’s testing found that ChatGPT couldn’t or didn’t detect which user is a child.

Oct 15 (Reuters) - The US Federal Trade Commission has sent civil subpoenas to AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI, seeking documents about safety incidents, Axios reported, citing a person familiar with the matter.
The probe comes amid mounting AI safety concerns after models reportedly hacked websites and behaved deceptively or aggressively in testing, highlighting the risks of increasingly autonomous systems and the adequacy of safeguards against harm.
Last month, Reuters reported that the FTC planned an industry-wide investigation into AI companies.
The FTC also plans to compel executives at top AI developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI and the research group METR to testify.
An OpenAI spokesperson said the company "will engage constructively with the FTC and continue working with regulators and policymakers on policies that raise the safety bar."

The FTC and Anthropic did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Axios report.
The regulator's demands run to more than 50 pages each and seek information on security incidents, safeguards, marketing materials and privacy policies, the news website reported.

FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson suggested in an interview with Reuters last month that developers who instruct agents in cybersecurity tests that result in hacks should be liable for any harm they cause.

# Another Week of Lawsuits Piling Up at OpenAI
Tim Bernard, Justin Hendrix / Oct 18, 2026 A finger is poised to tap the ChatGPT app icon displayed on a smartphone screen in Creteil, France, on October 1, 2026, as OpenAI begins rolling out Dots in ChatGPT, its new system of autonomous AI agents. (Photo by Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via AP)

August’s landmark settlement with Meta may have only whetted the appetite of state attorneys general to take on Big Tech. This past Wednesday, eight state attorneys general — from Arizona , Arkansas , Idaho , Iowa , ​Kansas , Montana , Nebraska ​and West ⁠Virginia — announced new lawsuits against OpenAI, accusing the frontier lab of a variety of illegal activities, many of which echo the recently resolved claims against Meta. Although Wednesday’s actions by the state attorneys general were coordinated and share the same counsel — large identical passages appear in the lawsuits — the suits were filed separately.
The state suits may have attracted the most headlines, but they were not the only new legal claims against the company last week. On Tuesday, a proposed class action complaint was filed in the United States District Court in the Northern District of California on behalf of a mother and her two children concerning OpenAI’s acquisition of children's data. And on Wednesday, litigation and advocacy organization Tech Justice Law and co-counsel filed another four suits in San Francisco County, California on behalf of private individuals alleged to have been harmed by OpenAI’s products. That group has filed a dozen previous complaints with co-counsel against OpenAI in California State courts. Many of these have been consolidated as Judicial Council Coordination Proceeding No. 5431, and the advocacy organization expects the new cases to also join this proceeding.
In June, Florida also sued OpenAI grounded in similar concerns. Many of the same claims are therefore set to be considered in parallel in nine different state courts. This article will lay out the cases made in these new lawsuits.

# The lawsuits

# State attorneys general · Filed Oct. 14, 2026

# Private lawsuits

- Gates v. OpenAI James Gates · San Francisco Superior Court · Oct. 14, 2026 PDF

# The attorneys general lawsuits

# What do the new suits allege?
The primary charge in the lawsuits is that OpenAI made unfounded claims of safety when its products were, in fact, harmful. In particular, though to varying degrees, the suits emphasize claims made to parents and risks and incidents of harm that children are exposed to. (Also present is a parallel argument that the company falsely claims the product to be generally “trustworthy and reliable.”)
The examples of harm given focus on the physical and on those that can lead to physical harm: promoting, assisting with, or failing to discourage violence and suicide, giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoias and delusions. Financial harms come up as well, including poor tax advice, and harms to critical thinking. Data collection, particularly from minors, is a recurring concern, and is reason for claims under state privacy law, such as in the Montana suit. Finally, the lawsuits also raise concerns about ‘rogue’ agents committing computer crimes or otherwise acting deceptively or maliciously against the intention of the user. Here, they cite OpenAI’s own recent admissions related to the Hugging Face incident; Iowa brings a separate count over OpenAI’s testing of autonomous agents.
OpenAI is accused of putting up a façade of safety through a host of measures, including its largely abandoned non-profit status; an unfulfilled pledge to direct a larger proportion of its compute resources towards safety research; and even the 12+ and 13+ age classification it claimed for its app. Complaints also point out that some guardrails are easy to circumvent. Multiple whistleblowers and other internal watchdogs have indicated that OpenAI should be aware of the dangers in their products but is failing to effectively mitigate them, and instead has been hurtling from one model release to the next with insufficient safety testing.
In a claim highly reminiscent of those against social media companies, the States also hold up the sycophancy of some of OpenAI’s models, along with their mimicry of human emotion, as evidence of the company working to manipulate users, juice engagement, and build dependency.
The secondary claim, again reminding us of the playbook against Meta, is that OpenAI has been collecting and using children’s data without proper consent and without taking appropriate steps to assess if users are indeed children.

# What laws may have been violated?
As they have been filed with reference to state and not federal law, the lawsuits’ details here do vary a little. The allegations of falsely claiming safety (and reliability) or other kinds of deception are brought with respect to consumer protection and deceptive trade practices laws. The use of children’s data may fall under general data privacy laws or child-specific ones. Nebraska also has an Age-Appropriate Online Design Code law that includes privacy, advertising, deceptive design, and addictive design measures.
Aside from these jurisdiction-specific laws, claims are brought under common law, including (at least in some states) negligence, liability for defective design and for failure to warn, unjust enrichment, and public nuisance.

# What relief is being sought?
The requests for relief also vary significantly between the states, in part due to the different legal environments. Monetary relief is sought in several different ways: damages, penalties when included in the relevant laws, disgorgement for gains that OpenAI made through illegal business practices, and reimbursement for those who paid for a product that was being misrepresented.
The states are also seeking a range of injunctive relief orders, including, as well as the end to some of the practices described above, deletion of user data, and the imposition of age assurance and other safety measures. Some states go even further, asking courts to order a pause in model testing and development until safeguards are in place (in some cases specifying models capable of recursive self-improvement — Arkansas seeks to “Enjoin Defendants from creating models capable of recursive self-improvement until they can ensure that such models will be aligned with human values”), or imposing monitoring and incident reporting requirements.
OpenAI issued a statement following the announcement of the lawsuits, saying it has “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack.” Company spokesperson Drew Pusateri said, “We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry, not just one company.”

# The Tech Justice Law lawsuits

# What do the new suits allege?
On Wednesday, Tech Justice Law filed a suit with the law firm Normand, Judkins & Couch in a California Superior Court on behalf of James Gates, a North Carolina man who alleges his estranged wife, Cheryl, used ChatGPT to concoct a plan to poison him. According to the complaint, ChatGPT “validated, amplified, and escalated” Cheryl’s concerns about her marriage to James. The chatbot then coached her on how to purchase, prepare, and deliver substances to poison him, and how to destroy digital evidence. James fell ill in July 2025, and Cheryl was indicted for attempted first-degree murder. (Notably, the chatbot assured Cheryl that deleted ChatGPT conversations are “unrecoverable,” even with a subpoena, which the suit notes is a “patently false representation of ChatGPT’s own data-retention practices.”)

AI services are unlikely to deliver enough revenue to cover the expected capital expenditure going into IT infrastructure between now and 2030, and it looks like neocloud operators will largely bow out or be bought out.
This is the conclusion from Gartner, which has added up the anticipated investments in AI datacenters over the next several years, estimated the revenue that can be expected from AI-driven applications over the same period, and found the numbers come up short.
Gartner's data comes from a report, "Prepare for AI Market Consolidation: Capital Write-Downs Could Exceed $4 Trillion by 2032 ," which concludes that AI will not generate enough sales to profitably cover all of the planned AI capital spending before 2032 at the earliest. But forecasts typically focus on the end of the decade, so it ran the numbers for 2030 as well.

REG AD

"In 2026, AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure, and are forecast to invest an additional $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030," said Gartner senior director analyst Will Sommer.

REG AD

"However, our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures during this period."
Assuming a 12 percent return on invested capital (ROIC), which many companies are said to regard as the bar for acceptability, Gartner estimates AI datacenter operators would need to generate a total of $8.5 trillion in revenue to cover capital spending and financing costs while achieving that return.
Unfortunately, it forecasts that the total enterprise and consumer AI revenue that can be attributed to AI datacenters during this period will add up to no more than $3.6 trillion.
Returns below expectations could force operators to write down assets whose value they can no longer recover, particularly as newer GPUs displace older hardware.
The result will be a shake-out of the companies providing AI infrastructure services, and Gartner believes that neocloud operators – "GPU-as-a-service" providers specializing in AI compute – will be the hardest hit. It forecasts that 80 percent of them won't survive as independent companies beyond 2030.
"Not everyone is in trouble," Sommer told The Register . "Some will outperform, some will underperform, and some will have to exit the market."
Gartner expects the hyperscalers to weather the shake-out better because their businesses extend beyond AI services.
Last year, McKinsey & Company warned that neocloud companies need to move up the AI stack and diversify to avoid being commoditized.

REG AD

There has been growing unease in the financial markets over the amount of capex being poured into AI investment, with some money lenders starting to get cold feet.
Last month, SoftBank Group found itself facing higher borrowing costs as the tech investment biz sought to drum up further funding for OpenAI.
Financial biz Jefferies issued a report this week saying that developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic are facing threats to their profitability from open source and Chinese models that undercut them on price.
Management consultant Bain & Company also published a report last month estimating that the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep up funding for the infrastructure needed to meet anticipated demand. Bain also forecast a revenue shortfall unless the industry develops products and use cases not yet identified.
Both the IMF and the Bank for International Settlements have voiced concerns about the AI bubble bursting and the effects rippling out across the global economy. ®

A financial analyst is questioning whether the collapse in AI costs owing to the arrival of Chinese, low-cost and open source models will cause a “reset” in the AI story as cloud providers struggle to recoup trillions of dollars of capital spending.
In a recent research note focused on Asian markets, Jefferies estimates that about half of the roughly $2.3 trillion contracted backlog at Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Oracle is owned by OpenAI and Anthropic. Yet Chinese AI models, open source/weight and small language models, threaten to undercut the prices the two US leaders charge, casting doubt on their future revenue.
Jefferies points to research from global aggregator platform OpenRouter, which found Chinese models processed 76.12 trillion tokens in the week ended 27 September, up from just 4.37 trillion in late April. The top four US providers processed 14.2 trillion tokens. Meanwhile, the launch of Moonshot AI’s open source Kimi K3 is “competing at the frontier” with an estimated 95 percent of the performance of Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.

REG AD

“The question now is whether all of the above has been priced fully into markets. This writer does not think so,” the Jefferies paper states.

REG AD

The largest hyperscalers are set to collectively spend between $600 and $800 billion this year on building datacenters, funding it increasingly with debt rather than cash. Jefferies, however, questions where the hyperscalers' future revenue streams will come from.
“It can no longer be assumed, most particularly with the arrival of the likes of Kimi K3, that large language models will ever be profitable given the related ongoing collapse in token pricing. This is extremely relevant for the hyperscalers since they have invested in datacenter capacity on the assumption that the compute will be purchased by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI,” the paper says.
While the long term bet on AI may be sound, in the medium term, there is a lot of uncertainty, it argues. “The AI story will be due for a big reset at some point in the not-so-distant future. Are the four hyperscalers really going to spend $993 billion on capex in 2027?” Jefferies questions.
There are also important questions to ask about how much of the hyperscalers’ reported profits are down to their investments in AI model builders on which they will also depend for revenue. “Other income and expenses” — which describes gains in investments — have spiked in importance. Jefferies says these investments are “likely to include positions in unlisted AI-related stocks.”
While the four major hyperscalers’ annualized earnings increased by $222 billion to reach $581 billion in the four quarters to 2Q26, “other non-operating income/loss” accounted for all of that increase, according to the analyst. Jefferies says “other non-operating income/loss” increased by $224 billion year-on-year to $237 billion over the same period, meaning it accounted "for all of the increase in earnings."
Other research has underlined how much revenue and borrowing cloud providers might need to fund their datacenter building plans. The 2026 annual Global Technology Report from management consultants Bain & Company says the AI industry must generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding the infrastructure needed to meet anticipated demand. That means the industry will need new uses beyond employee productivity.
Bain suspects existing AI applications might make up $1.8 trillion in revenue, but this still leaves a $4.2 trillion shortfall. It could be plugged by emerging AI applications such as search engines and ads, AI-built autonomous vehicles, and AI simulations. Even if they work out, these new categories will only add up to $1.5 trillion in revenue, leaving a $2.7 trillion gap which might be filled by “new products and uses that don’t exist today.”

The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.
In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.
“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, and the UK and euro area potentially more insulated – though investors with US holdings would be hit.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, the deputy director of the IMF’s monetary and capital department, launching the report, said: “The exposure of the rest of the world to US assets, particularly AI, is the highest it has ever been. So this is supporting the global economy through wealth effects today; but if we get a market correction it could have broad implications.”
An AI crash was one of three “salient risks” to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack.
It called this trio of factors “plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”.
The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector.
“Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures, and circular financing arrangements,” it said.
Such a reassessment would then “sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers”.
The “magnificent seven” big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35% of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12% a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50% in the past two years.
Yet the IMF warned of “growing evidence” that the successful rollout of AI “may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by ‘hyperscaler’ firms”, and “potential economic gains may not be as large as expected”.
The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle.
Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers. Reports that the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT was making good progress on a new chip architecture also hit South Korean tech companies.
The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash.
In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves; hedge fund investment in the sector; and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks.
In the event of an AI-led market downturn “these growing sources of leverage heighten the potential for forced selling and surges in equity volatility”, it said.
It also pointed to the prevalence of “circular financing” deals , tying stronger AI companies to weaker partners in the same sector, and potentially exacerbating the impact of a share price correction.
It identified $300bn (£227bn) worth of transactions between hyperscalers and “weaker AI firms” in just the past three years, supplemented by $650bn in debt, in exchange for $1.4tn in future financial commitments.
In London, the chief executive of the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, Nikhil Rathi, urged every small business across the financial sector to take out insurance to protect themselves against AI-related cybersecurity threats.
He told MPs on the Commons Treasury committee that not all companies would have the resources to pay for access to “frontier” AI models such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which has been released on a restricted basis after it was said to be rapidly identifying gaps in government and corporate cybersecurity systems.
“One message I’d give to every small business: you should consider making sure you are insured,” Rathi said.

Anthropic, the developer of the Claude artificial intelligence model, is facing questions over slowing growth. Revenue rose steadily through the third quarter of this year, but the pace of expansion fell sharply. Investors have lowered their valuation of the company amid the controversy, which comes as Anthropic prepares for an initial public offering as early as next month, according to reports. Market watchers said doubts that had been building around the company surfaced all at once with the latest earnings disclosure.
The biggest concern in the market is the marked slowdown in Anthropic's revenue growth rate, according to foreign news reports compiled as of the 15th. Anthropic recently told investors that third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion, extending gains from $4.8 billion in the first quarter and $11.6 billion in the second, the Financial Times and other outlets reported. The quarterly revenue increase was $5.2 billion in the third quarter, down more than $1 billion from $6.8 billion in the prior period. The revenue growth rate fell to 45% from 142% over the same period, a drop of 98 percentage points.
Anthropic sought to reassure investors by pointing to an adjusted operating margin of 11%, but some investors have begun discussing a valuation of around $1.5 trillion for the company, Reuters reported on the same day. That marks a 25% reduction from the previous valuation of $2 trillion.

The loss of customers, partly by choice and partly not, is another factor. Meta and Microsoft switched to their own models or cheaper open-source alternatives to cut the high cost of Anthropic's Claude, The Information reported on the 6th.
Anthropic has cracked down on what it says are efforts by DeepSeek, Alibaba and others to copy its models through distillation, a technique that collects responses from another model and uses them for training. At the latest investor briefing, Anthropic said distillation-related revenue accounted for 5% to 7% of its total and that it had cut this significantly in the third quarter — an explanation that backfired. Business Insider noted that protecting its own technology had hurt revenue growth.
Anthropic's method of calculating annualized revenue, which multiplies a given month's revenue by 12, has also come under renewed scrutiny. As of July this year, Anthropic's annualized revenue stood at $65 billion. With monthly revenue rising 57% to 58% in April and May, investors expected full-year revenue to reach $100 billion to $120 billion even if growth slowed to 9% to 10% for the remainder of the year. That projection underpinned the company's $2 trillion valuation. The latest briefing, however, confirmed that the growth rate had instead declined. Market research firm SemiAnalysis lowered its annualized revenue estimate for Anthropic to about $74 billion based on the newly disclosed results. Critics also say the differing revenue formulas used by Anthropic and rival OpenAI are a tactic that prevents comparison between the two privately held companies.
A lukewarm market response to Anthropic's IPO could weigh on the broader AI market. Investors see the near-term outlook for the AI market as hinging largely on whether Anthropic's IPO succeeds and on OpenAI's planned listing next year.

# Investing in the public benefit
Oct 18, 2026

Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

New York — Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose more than 45% to $16.8bn from the previous quarter, according to an investor who attended a pre-IPO meeting with Anthropic leadership in San Francisco on Wednesday.
Revenue in the first quarter was $4.7bn, and $11.6bn in the second quarter, according to the person who attended the investor day meant to familiarise prospective Anthropic investors before its highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO).
The IPO is expected to precede a public listing by rival OpenAI, making Anthropic an early test of investor appetite for heavily unprofitable AI developers pursuing massive scale. Its public-market debut is likely to be pushed until after the November US midterm elections.
Scrutiny of AI companies’ finances has intensified as they pour money into chips, data centers and computing power needed to develop and operate increasingly powerful models.

Founded by former OpenAI executives, Anthropic has emerged as one of the leading generative AI developers with its Claude family of models. Its expansion has been underpinned by Alphabet’s Google and Amazon, which are simultaneously investors, suppliers of computing power and important distribution partners, as well as AI competitors.
Anthropic has also sought to distinguish itself through its focus on AI safety , warning of the dangers posed by increasingly capable systems even as it competes in the race to develop and commercialise more powerful models.
Its research has found that its own AI agents have engaged in troubling behaviour in test environments, including leaking sensitive information and sabotaging code, though the company has said it has not seen evidence of such misalignment in real-world deployments.

Gemini 4 Argon is a step forward in what models can do — especially when it comes to deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. Its cyberdefense capabilities are frontier-level and designed to give defenders an advantage over attackers. To maximize its potential, we first wanted cyber defenders to put it to work via our Fairwind Program , while our own security teams used it to scan critical systems inside and outside of Google.
This window of limited access showed why these capabilities matter. For instance, Wiz used Argon to uncover a critical bug in hospital software that previous models had missed, helping protect hundreds of thousands of patient records. Meanwhile, Google’s own security teams used Argon to find and patch bugs across internal software or open-source software. This included fixing foundational vulnerabilities affecting systems globally, which are going through our responsible disclosure process.
Today, we are beginning to roll out Argon broadly , as well as expanding our Fairwind Program to additional trusted cyber defenders. To do this well, we grappled with two big questions:

- How do we build the right safety guardrails? If Argon can help defenders find complex software bugs or help scientists design experiments, how do we stop bad actors from using it to launch cyberattacks or create biological threats? ( Misuse )

- Can we trust the model to do the job the right way? As models become more resourceful problem-solvers, how do we make sure they don’t cut corners, cross boundaries, or make incorrect high-stakes decisions? ( Misalignment and Prompt Injection )
Our full Safety and Security Report systematically covers our set of defenses. Below are some highlights from how we approached these two questions for Gemini 4 Argon.

# Misuse prevention across high-risk domains
The same coding and reasoning improvements that enabled Argon to find and patch vulnerabilities also drove better performance on our cybersecurity tests — solving all 12 of the end-to-end simulated cyberattack scenarios, up from five in our previous generation. In biology evaluations, unguarded versions of the model also showed a much stronger ability to help troubleshoot complex lab procedures step by step. Following our Frontier Safety Framework , since we saw elevated capabilities in the cyber and biological domains, we put our next-generation set of frontier safeguards in place across both areas.
First, when it comes to potentially dangerous requests — from writing exploit code to helping with dangerous biological materials, Argon is significantly better at not fulfilling harmful requests than our previous models. On an adversarial set meant to stress test the model, violations reduced nearly twofold — also significantly better than previous Gemini models. Second, we wrap the model in three layers of real-time protection; this is to prevent determined attackers that might try to jailbreak (i.e. trick) the model by disguising a dangerous request as a harmless story or breaking it into dozens of small questions over several weeks. Here is how these protections work:

- Input screening: Smaller models check incoming requests and conversation context for malicious intent or dangerous requests.

- Internal introspection: Even if a request is cleverly disguised to look harmless, small transformers ("activation probes") read the model’s internal neural signals and are trained to spot when it is activating knowledge about cyberattacks or biological threats.

- Continuous monitoring: As the model reasons and writes its response across multiple steps, we combine these signals and take action when necessary such as cutting off the agent mid-stream if the responses become problematic.
Combining real-time protection, faster fixes for new jailbreaks and enhanced monitoring for recurring misuse has made our systems better at preventing real-world harm. For instance, external bio jailbreak red teaming could only unlock less than 1% of bio sub-tasks we test for.

# Real-time misalignment monitoring
Misalignment can sometimes mean an agent deciding on its own to pursue a goal different to what was intended by the user. Because Argon is much better than earlier models at understanding the environment it is running in, we test carefully for that kind of behavior. For example, we ran realistic "honeypot" tests to see if the model would increase its ability to take covert actions, such as sabotaging safety monitoring. We didn't find any instances of that behavior.
But what we do see in practice today is something much more familiar: an agent trying too hard to finish the job it was given. When a resourceful assistant is told to get a task done and runs into a locked door, it can treat that obstacle as just another puzzle to solve.
This is why we trained Gemini 4 Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause to ask for human confirmation. On coding benchmarks where models have no incentive to hold back, attempts to take a shortcut or cheat on the task dropped to just 2% on Gemini 4 Argon, our best performance for recent Gemini models.
And while this is a major step forward, when a model runs millions of complex tasks, even a rare misstep will eventually show up. As a second line of defense, we built an automated misalignment monitor that reads both the agent’s actions and its internal "scratchpad" (its step-by-step chain of thought) in real time, blocking severe boundary violations before they happen and flagging serious internal cases for human responders. (We continually harden our training and evaluation environments against potential escapes. You can read more about this in our agent control roadmap ). We run this monitor in our products, on our internal coding agents, during our training runs, and during our capability evaluations.
When training tasks were difficult or when training environments were flawed, our monitor caught the model, in rare instances, creatively attempting to game the test. The model attempted to escalate container privileges to alter grading scripts, read answers from the test runner's memory, and in one case it even crashed the evaluation sandbox to avoid getting scored for a failed run. While we use these catches to fix flawed tasks, we do not use them to otherwise intervene with the training process to avoid overfitting to the monitor.
And we always follow one rule: we don’t penalize the model for what it writes in its chain of thought during training . Here’s an example to illustrate why: in a reinforcement learning training run where a shortcut penalty was accidentally applied to the chain of thought, openly discussed shortcuts dropped by 61%, but that did not mean the model took less shortcuts. Instead, the share of shortcuts the model took silently — without mentioning them in its thoughts — more than tripled (from 11.2% to 36.4%). Avoiding thought penalties encourages the model’s reasoning to stay transparent and monitorable.

# Prompt injection resistance

# An update on independent evaluators
Oct 15, 2026

Last month, we committed to stronger independent, third-party assessment of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from METR , a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.

METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on several reviews of our Risk Reports . We’re also working with SecureBio and Accenture as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face .

Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.

# Why we work with independent evaluators
As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.

To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:

- Expertise in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as alignment faking .

- Independence : they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.

- Enough access to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.

- Freedom to publish observations and assessments of a model or a process.

Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.

For the AI industry, this is a step toward robust safety oversight . We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.

# What we mean by “employee-like access”
We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk. 1
METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into predefined categories such as reproducing confidential IP. (Anthropic ultimately decides what information does and does not fall into these categories, although METR reserves the right to make certain statements about the level of access and information it received.) 2
Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.

# Our other evaluator partnerships
We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.

We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.

In the first tier, evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.

In the second tier, evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.

The third tier is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.

SecureBio is in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our August Risk Report , after completing and publishing a pilot review of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access. 3

#
What testing revealed about super intelligence in OT

In our testing, frontier super intelligence navigated unfamiliar industrial systems, adapted when blocked, and moved physical equipment within minutes. For OT defenders, that can mean less time to detect and stop digital access from becoming physical action.


#
Speed Read ↗︎

- Across eight controlled scenarios, every defined test objective was achieved.


- In one test, models progressed from perimeter compromise to actions inside the industrial control network in just over 16 minutes. In another, a model identified and moved a robotic arm within minutes.


- Existing defenses blocked or slowed some actions, but no single safeguard consistently stopped the models from reaching their objectives.




Just 16 minutes and change. That is how long it took frontier super intelligence models in one controlled test to move from a perimeter compromise to actions inside an industrial control network. In another scenario, a model found a robotic arm, mapped its protection zones and motion limits, and moved it within minutes.

The models did this without source code, engineering documents, or advanced OT guidance. Across eight scenarios, every defined test objective was achieved. More important, the models connected work that usually spans multiple people and stages, including asset discovery, device research, attack planning, troubleshooting, and execution. Building on Booz Allen’s Cyber Weapon Index , this research extends our examination of super intelligence-enabled offensive capabilities beyond enterprise networks and into operational technology (OT), where cyber actions can directly affect machinery and industrial processes.

Testing took place in Booz Allen’s isolated OT Cybersecurity Lab, where human operators approved every exploit and any action that could produce a physical effect. The consequences at an operating facility would depend on its architecture, equipment, safeguards, and the access an attacker obtained. Within the lab, the models showed how quickly partial network access could open paths to machinery and industrial processes.


#
What the Testing Showed

Booz Allen tested frontier models in a multi-vendor lab modeled on a manufacturing facility. The models identified equipment they had not encountered before, matched asset and firmware details to known vulnerabilities, built attack paths, reached controllers and supervisory systems, and, when authorized, changed physical equipment.

Two tests showed how the models responded when the environment did not behave as expected. In one, a model noticed a safety relay repeatedly searching for a missing communications partner. From that clue, it identified a possible way to impersonate the missing peer. In the SCADA test, the models initially targeted the wrong version of the operator interface. They checked active sessions, found the version used in the control room, revised the payload, and discovered live, pre-authenticated connections to 14 OT devices.

Some controls did exactly what they were meant to do. A controller rejected a stop command, and a motor set to local control would not start remotely. Firewalls, segmentation, and endpoint protection slowed or blocked other actions. The models sometimes switched methods or followed another application path, so no single safeguard provided consistent protection across the evaluation.


#
What OT Leaders Should Do Now

The tests identified several places defenders can intervene, slow an attack, or stop it entirely.


- Cut off easy routes. Segment around high-consequence processes and remove dual-homed systems, shared services, and pre-authenticated sessions that cross security boundaries.




- Secure the systems that bridge the environment. Pay particular attention to firewalls, switches, jump hosts, administrative interfaces, SCADA platforms, and engineering workstations.




- Prioritize what could lead to a physical consequence. A severity score tells only part of the story. Trace what an attacker could reach from the vulnerable system and what that access could change.




- Monitor operational changes and prepare to restore. Watch for controller-mode changes, program writes, SCADA project imports, and unexpected use of trusted interfaces. Keep tested backups and known-good configurations ready.


- Monitor operational changes and prepare to restore. Watch for controller-mode changes, program writes, SCADA project imports, and unexpected use of trusted interfaces. Keep tested backups and known-good configurations ready.




- Some of the clearest evidence came from what the models could not do. One controller refused a stop command. A motor in local-control mode could not be started remotely. Those failures show why device configuration and local safety controls matter even after an intruder reaches OT.
